1029-the-night-born:
Jack London gathers here a set of short tales from the edge of civilized life: prospectors, sailors, prize-fighters, and men who test themselves against cold, sea, and greed. The title points to those born, as London saw it, to roam by night and live by nerve rather than by rule. The stories range from the far north to the warm seas.

London's people face stark choices, and luck or pluck decides them in a few hard pages. His prose is blunt and fast, with a taste for strong men and stronger fates. The book shows his range beyond his famous dog tales, and it rewards readers who like short, sharp yarns.
10451-life-of-johnson-volume-5-tour-to-t:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson, edited by George Birkbeck Hill, continues in this fifth volume with two journeys. One is the tour to the Hebrides in 1773. The other is Johnson's diary of a journey into North Wales in 1774. Boswell traveled with Johnson to Scotland, recording talk, anecdotes, and opinions of men and books along the way.

The volume adds Johnson's own poems on the tour, never before published. It also gives an authentic account of the escape of the grandson of James II in 1746. Hebridean islands, Welsh roads, and Johnson's conversation fill the pages. Readers get a classic travel biography, full of wit, landscape, and eighteenth-century life.
11327-english-literature-modern:
G. H. Mair's English Literature: Modern, in the Home University Library, surveys English writing from the Renaissance to the present age in ten short chapters. Elizabethan poetry and prose, the drama, the seventeenth century, the age of good sense, Dr. Johnson, the Romantic revival, the Victorian age, and the novel each get a chapter, with a bibliography and chronological table. First printed in 1911 and revised in 1914, the book was meant for general readers.

Mair opens by comparing literary ages to moments of sudden widening in a person's life, when new possibilities bring fresh endeavor. His judgments are brisk and confident, in the style of the series. Students still find the volume a useful short map of the field, even where later scholarship has revised its verdicts.
12190-the-adventures-of-captain-horn:
Frank R. Stockton published The Adventures of Captain Horn in 1910, an adventure novel that begins with a shipwreck and grows into a treasure hunt. Stockton, known for The Lady, or the Tiger, here mixes sea yarn with business comedy.

Captain Horn and his party, cast ashore in South America, face the Rackbirds, a gang of outlaws, and discover a hidden hoard. Chapters follow an introductory disaster, new faces in camp, a cliff scheme, and a pile of fuel that hides more than warmth. Horn must get his people home, guard the treasure, and deal honestly with partners and claimants. The novel is brisk and inventive, with Stockton usual calm narration of wild events.
12327-the-jewish-manual-practical-inform:
Edited by a lady and published in London in 1846, The Jewish Manual offers practical information in Jewish and modern cookery, with recipes and hints relating to the toilette. The editor preface notes that existing culinary works give no insight into the Hebrew kitchen.

Most cookbooks, she argues, are valueless to the Jewish housekeeper because of prohibited articles and combinations. The manual therefore gives kosher recipes, including Molina pie: minced cold veal or chicken with smoked beef or tongue, seasoned, simmered in gravy, and bound with egg yolks. It also covers table manners and dress. The book is an early English Jewish cookbook, practical, pioneering, and proud of its kitchen.
12777-the-young-engineers-in-nevada-or-s:
Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton try their luck as mining engineers in Nevada in this Hancock adventure. A boy named Alf, a trail camp, and Jim Ferrers, who becomes their partner, set the story going. Claims, new owners, and a rival named Dolph Gage test their nerve, while snow, wolves, and a signal of distress raise the stakes.

After losing the best claim in the district by being too slow, Tom resolves that they will stake their fortunes on the turn of a pick, working their own mines in earnest. Harry, at first downcast, falls in with the plan. The tale pairs mining craft with pluck and partnership.
12930-publications-of-the-scottish-histo:
Volume thirty-six of the Scottish History Society publications prints the journals of Sir John Lauder, Lord Fountainhall, from 1665 to 1676, edited by Donald Crawford. Journals in France, journeys in London, Oxford, and Scotland, and a chronicle of the Court of Session fill the volume. Observations on public affairs, accounts, a book catalogue, and a letter to his son complete it.

A Bedlam story shows the period flavour: a man who believed his head was glass was cured when attendants broke glass before him, proving the glass, not his head, had shattered. Fountainhall's notes give Restoration Scotland in a lawyer's sharp eye. The volume serves historians of seventeenth-century Scotland.
13077-wild-western-scenes-a-narrative-of:
J. B. Jones's narrative, first entered in 1856 and reissued in a revised stereotype edition in 1875, centers on Daniel Boone, the famed American pioneer. Jones frames Boone's exploits with tales of bear, deer, and buffalo hunts, wolf hunts, fishing, fights with Native peoples, and meetings with snakes. Sixteen engravings from original designs illustrate the text.

The story is told by a party traveling the western wilds, with Boone as guide and hero, and a talkative companion named Joe for comic relief. Campfire talk, strange sounds in the air, and sudden alarms on the trail fill the chapters. Jones wrote for readers hungry for frontier adventure, and his Boone is less a man of record than a legend made to carry the whole West.
13115-anahuac-or-mexico-and-the-mexicans:
Edward Burnett Tylor's 1861 travel book follows a route from Cuba through Yucatan and Vera Cruz into the heart of Mexico. Its chapter headings run from Cuban railways and pirates to Mexican politics, Aztec remains, aloe fields, and mud-brick houses. Tylor, later a founder of anthropology, writes as a curious traveler with an eye for custom.

He notes drinkers who take spirits hour by hour, potters at Soquital, and salt carriers on the road. A night ride brings a grand sight: grass fire sweeping a hillside, throwing light over smoke and cloud. Tylor mixes ancient and modern Mexico at every step, and the book remains a lively, if dated, portrait of a country on the edge of change.
14338-books-and-habits-from-the-lectures:
John Erskine chose and edited these lectures by Lafcadio Hearn, printed in 1922. Hearn taught English letters in Japan, and spoke to students who met Western books across a gap of tongue and custom. The lectures ask what makes a book hard to grasp, and how taste grows. They range over old Norse tales, French verse, and English prose. Hearn's voice is that of a teacher who loves books and trusts reading.

One lecture weighs Norse feud law, where a killing called for vengeance unless a blood price was paid. Hearn notes that kin seldom felt paid off by coin alone, so feuds could run for years. Another lecture lingers on a French poem about a cicada that sings till it dies on a stalk. Hearn glosses the word encolure, the line of neck and shoulder, for which English has no twin. The book opens two far-apart literatures through talk.
14844-the-taming-of-red-butte-western:
Francis Lynde's western, published by Scribner in 1916 from a 1910 copyright, sets out to tame Red Butte. Collars and cuffs, the red desert, a little brother of the cows and the Rio Gloria open a story of ranching, rail and rough men.

Outlaws, everyman's share, a killer, bridge timbers, Judson's joke and Flemister follow, with nemesis, pleasurers, bitter-sweet, blind signals and Eleanor intervening. A shadowgraph closes the arc. Dedicated to Charles Augustine Stickle, brother in deed though not by blood, the tale of his birthland mixes romance with the hard work of bringing order to a wild valley.
1620-the-lion-and-the-unicorn:
Richard Harding Davis's Lion and the Unicorn gathers stories dedicated to Lt-Col Arthur H. Lee, British military attache with the United States Army, in memory of hot days and hot corners. The title tale follows Prentiss, who holds a long lease on a house, through a story of empire, love, and war.

Other tales, from On the Fever Ship to The Last Ride Together, move between soldiers, sailors, and correspondents at the edge of empire. Davis writes with dash and sentiment. The collection is a period book of adventure, vivid in its day and still readable for its energy.
16343-beth-woodburn:
Maud Petitt's Beth Woodburn, published in Toronto in 1897 by William Briggs, was the author's first book, lovingly dedicated to her mother. It opens in Briarsfield, a pretty village in Norfolk County close to Lake Erie's shore, already grown almost to town size and dignity. Chapter one finds Beth at eighteen, and later chapters follow a dream of life, a question of whither Beth, Marie, love, varsity days, and an ending.

Death, love, and farewell mark the later chapters, as Beth grows from village girlhood toward adult choice. Petitt writes gentle Canadian domestic fiction in a clear, warm style. Readers who like coming-of-age tales from small-town Ontario will find a tender first novel.
18256-woodside-or-look-listen-and-learn:
Caroline Hadley, author of Children's Sayings and Stories of Old, wrote this children's nature book, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1902. Woodside, or Look, Listen, and Learn, opens with Longfellow's verses on Nature as an old nurse who takes a child upon her knee and shows a story book written by the Father. The book asks children to wander, look, and listen.

Chapters bring grandpapa's house, listening in the woods, and Tom's birds' eggs. Jack and the gardener, hiving the bees, and wasps and their ways follow. Charley Foster's pets, a talk with Aunt Lizzie, and after the rain close the set. Illustrations show the arrival at grandpapa's, the visit to the watch-dog, and the visit to the pony. Children get nature study as a visit: animals, bees, and woods met at a grandparent's house.
18458-star-born:
Andre Norton wrote this science fiction novel, published by Ace Books in New York. Star Born opens with a question from Tas Kordov's Record of the First Years. What of the children born on a new world? They will have no memories of Terra's green hills and blue seas. Will they be Terrans, or something else? The novel takes up that question as its theme.

The story opens with travelers sighting a cove from the sea, the first break in a cliff wall guarding a continent's interior. Dalgard Nordis, son of the colony, steers an outrigger with Sssuri in the bow, two voyagers of different race and species working without words, as if bound by a rapport beyond speech. Readers get a colony world seen through its second generation: exploration, alien friendship, and the making of a new people.
18565-a-little-swiss-sojourn:
W. D. Howells wrote this travel book, published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1893, with illustrations of Montreux, Villeneuve, the Castle of Chillon, and markets at Vevay. The book records eighty or ninety days passed in Switzerland, told in papers that follow the author's stay by the lake.

The first paper opens at the White Cross Inn, with tourists at Montreux and the road to Villeneuve. Howells writes of haymaking in the marshes, washing clothes in the lake, fountains, wine-presses, and bargains before a notary, giving a gentle, observant picture of Swiss town life in summer.
18855-the-return:
H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire published this science fiction story in Astounding Science Fiction in January 1954. It opens with a survey team in a helicopter over a yellow-brown river, eating a makeshift meal of smoked pork and rice. The crew, including Altamont and Loudons, is exploring country far from home.

The team soon finds a small, isolated group living on its own, whose religion strikes the visitors as strange, yet logical on its own terms. The story turns on that meeting: how a cut-off community keeps its beliefs, and how outsiders judge them. Readers get a short tale of exploration and cultural contact, told with Piper's usual care for practical detail.
19158-the-return:
H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire wrote this science fiction tale, The Return, first printed in The Science-Fictional Sherlock Holmes in 1960. Altamont flies a helicopter over a yellow-brown river, eating a meal of smoked pork chops, rice, egg powder, and milk fried in bacon grease, cooked by Loudons from leftovers. The scene is a settled, walled town called the Toon.

Elders test young men with constant checks, while a leader of the Irregulars weighs whether to move the Toon, with its graves, walls, and houses that cannot travel. Theological disputes over sacred books add tension. Readers get a thoughtful post-collapse tale of tradition, leadership, and change.
19691-dead-man-s-plack-and-an-old-thorn:
A plack was an old Scots coin of small worth. Dead Man's Plack and An Old Thorn pairs two works of English local lore and nature writing. One passage follows a watcher haunting a spot day after day. He pursues small creatures, not to kill and cabinet them. He wants only to witness the comedy of their bright little lives.

That watcher sums up the book's spirit: patient, fond, and exact. English nature writing of this school prized the small and near. A thorn tree or a dead man's coin could anchor real feeling. The pieces reward slow reading. They record a countryside world that was already passing when they were written.
21058-the-strange-adventures-of-eric-bla:
Eric Blackburn, fourth officer of the steamship Saturn, tells his own story in Harry Collingwood's sea novel. When the Saturn is lost in mid-ocean, Blackburn is the sole survivor. A passing sailing ship picks him up, and he soon finds himself raised to skipper.

Blackburn joins a search for hidden treasure, and the search succeeds. On the way to port the ship is wrecked on an uncharted island. There he and the dead captain's son explore and meet a local king. They help that king fight off attacks by huge apes, then guard their treasure from two shady former crewmen.
21702-shifting-winds-a-tough-yarn:
Several linked tales run side by side in this sea story by R. M. Ballantyne, the Scottish writer of boys' adventure books. One thread follows the seaman Gaff and his son Billy, and another follows Mrs. Gaff at home. Captain Bingley, his son Gildart, the Stuart family, and a man named Haco Barepoles fill out the cast.

Most of the action stays ashore, in the small fishing village of Wreckumoft and the town of Athenbury. The book also shows the work of a charity that aided shipwrecked sailors and fishermen. Ballantyne weaves the separate lives together and apart, and the whole story carries a clear Christian message about duty, loss, and help given to strangers.
21789-a-discourse-of-life-and-death-by-m:
Two French works in the English of the Countess of Pembroke make up this volume, printed at London in 1592. The first is Philippe de Mornay's Discourse of Life and Death, a grave prose meditation. Mornay wonders why men hurry toward rest in every task, yet fear the end of life's own hard voyage. Life, he writes, is a sea open to all winds and a web forever woven and undone.

The second piece is Antonius, a tragedy by Robert Garnier, retelling the fall of Antony in classical form. Mary Sidney, the countess, was among the finest translators of her age. Her versions brought French thought and drama to English readers. The old spelling and stately pace reward slow reading.
22124-the-golden-shoemaker-or-cobbler-ho:
J. W. Keyworth tells a village tale in The Golden Shoemaker, or "Cobbler" Horn. Horn works in the little shop behind his kitchen. His house holds only two rooms below and three small chambers above. In the room over the workshop his wife lies dying, and her coughing sounds through the boarded floor.

Around this poor home Keyworth builds a story of faith, neighbours, and quiet endurance. The cobbler's nickname, and the gold of the title, point to worth that money cannot measure. Such tales were written for Sunday reading and cottage shelves. Keyworth's is a plain, tender example of Victorian religious fiction at its most domestic.
22358-erik-dorn:
Ben Hecht wrote Erik Dorn, a novel published in 1921. Hecht was a Chicago newspaperman turning to fiction. His hero is glimpsed first in darkness, watching people drift past a lawn.

Dorn lowers his eyes toward the street beyond the lawn. Figures seem to float under the dark trees. He cannot see them distinctly as they pass. At moments a face rewards his stare: a featureless glint of white. Shadows move within a motionless darkness around him. That moody opening suits a novel of ambition and city life. Hecht's sharp prose made Erik Dorn an early success in American letters.
22544-a-world-is-born:
Leigh Brackett wrote A World Is Born, a science fiction story of Mercury. Gray's fury opens the tale, hotter than boiling springs. Those springs run from the Sunside to water the valleys.

Gray hated John Moulton and his daughter Jill bitterly. They had conceived a plan of building a new world there. Their settlers would be destitute and desperate veterans of war. The Second Interplanetary War left those veterans needing a home. Building one on Mercury's twilight belt is their gamble and hope. Brackett was a master of planetary romance in the pulps. Her tale mixes harsh scenery, old soldiers, and stubborn colonization dreams.
23028-greylorn:
Keith Laumer opens Greylorn with a bleak report. Scouts went out forty-three years ago to all twenty-five colony worlds planted during the last century's Colonial Era. With the last scouts home, Earth faced the truth. No help, the report concludes, exists out there from any of them.

Cut off and weakening, humanity in Laumer's tale must look elsewhere for the help it needs. Greylorn names the grim errand that follows, a mission into dangers the report only hints at. Laumer wrote taut, ironic space adventure, and this novella shows his economy. Every paragraph earns its keep. Readers get a hard future, plainly told, with the stakes set in the first page.
23995-the-land-of-the-kangaroo-adventure:
Thomas W. Knox published The Land of the Kangaroo in Boston in 1896, subtitled The Adventures of Two Youths in the Great Island Continent. Knox, author of In Wild Africa and the fifteen-volume Boy Travelers series, died ten days after completing the book, leaving his planned travel series unfinished.

The publishers announced that remaining volumes would be issued by another hand. With five illustrations by H. Burgess, including a ship becalmed in the doldrums, the book follows two youths through Australia, then rapidly rising in prominence among the colonies. For boy readers of the 1890s, it was a first-hand-feeling tour of a continent of strange beasts and wide distances.
24248-the-girl-scouts-good-turn:
Edith Lavell wrote this girls' school story, published by A. L. Burt Company in New York in 1922. It belongs to her Girl Scouts series, beside The Girl Scouts at Miss Allen's School, The Girl Scouts at Camp, The Girl Scouts' Canoe Trip, and The Girl Scouts' Rivals. The tale is set at Miss Allen's Boarding School, where the girls return for the fall term.

On the first Saturday of term, the sophomores prepare their reception for the freshmen, with Marjorie Wilkinson as chairman. The bare gymnasium vanishes under cedar branches, artificial snow, snowbanks, pine needles, and frosty tinsel, with a dancing space kept clear in the middle. Readers get a cheerful school story of planning, friendship, and a good turn done well.
24567-blind-man-s-lantern:
Allen Kim Lang wrote this short science-fiction story, first printed in Analog in December 1962 and illustrated by Schelling. Its premise is that successful colonies among the stars need interstellar ships, but they also need a rare sort of man, not the sort one might expect.

The story opens with an old village tale: a young man walking home in the dark meets a blind man carrying a lamp. The youngster shouts across the road, asking why a blind man needs light. Lang turns that parable into a story of space colonisation. Readers get a clever, humane tale about the unseen work that keeps a colony alive.
26342-chronicles-of-strathearn:
Chronicles of Strathearn, published at Crieff by David Philips in 1896 with pictures by W. B. MacDougall, gathers local history from many ministerial pens. Contents list Celtic saints and ancient churches, the Pictish capital, the historic presbytery of Auchterarder, memories of Gask, and the head of Strathearn. Later pieces cover the banks of the Devon, the well of Saint Fillan, the plain of the bards, and the abbey of Inchaffray.

A southern outpost on the Highland edge, the castle and sheriffdom of Auchterarder, and the gate of the Highlands close the set. The opening piece recalls sunset on the Knock of Crieff, with afterglow lying like purple mist from Ben Ledi to Comrie. The book gives a Scottish valley its past in short, vivid chapters.
26417-a-sheaf-of-corn:
Mary E. Mann's 1908 collection gathers short stories of English village life around the fictional Dulditch. The opening tale finds Dinah Brome in the village shop, watching the weighing of her weekly groceries with keen eyes. Strong and wholesome in looks, sober in dress, she pays well and constantly, yet the narrator insists she lacks any backbone of character.

Other stories follow a clerk, a tea-shop, a chalk mark on a gate, Freddy's ship, a nerve cure, a private ward, and Dora of the ringlets. Pink carnations, a little white dog, a broken boot, and the cares of a curate round out the sheaf. Mann's sketches are sharp, unsentimental, and fond of exposing the gap between respectable looks and inner worth.
26673-at-the-sign-of-the-jack-o-lantern:
Myrtle Reed published this novel with Grosset and Dunlap at New York, copyrighted in 1902, issued under arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. Reed was already known for Lavender and Old Lace, The Master's Violin, and A Spinner in the Sun. Its first chapter is called The End of the Honeymoon, and its last The Love of Another Elaine.

Dorothy and Harlan arrive by stage in a blinding storm at a queer house with eccentric outlines. The driver calls out good luck and the Jack-o'-Lantern as he leaves them. Matches sputter and fail in the empty, echoing rooms until a candle is found. Later chapters bring a first caller, finances, Mrs. Smithers, the coming of Elaine, an uninvited guest, Mrs. Dodd's husbands and fates, treasure-trove, and Uncle Ebeneezer's diary.
2766-the-red-acorn:
John McElroy wrote this Civil War novel of a young Union volunteer learning war the hard way. The red acorn of the title marks a corps badge, and the hero's journey runs from enlistment and fear through battle, shame, and hard won courage.

McElroy, himself a veteran, writes with blunt honesty about camp life, combat, and the men who broke or held. The novel mixes adventure with moral weight, and it avoids easy glory. It remains a respected story of the war from a private's view, told by one who knew it.
29038-in-the-orbit-of-saturn:
R. F. Starzl wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Astounding Stories in October 1931. Its note promises that an agent of the Interplanetary Flying Police, disguised as a willing prisoner aboard a pirate ship, will unravel the mystery of the dreaded Solar Scourge. Aboard the Celestia, gliding toward Titan, Saturn's major moon, the tale opens when the ship falters and its rotation stops.

Passengers drift from the curved floor in helpless confusion as gravity fails, and a dark mass blots the stars at the portholes. An old man cries that pirates have come, fearing ransom will break his company, while his young companion answers with annoyance. Readers get a brisk space-pirate adventure, with a secret agent, a seized liner, and the Solar Scourge waiting beyond Saturn.
29205-grove-of-the-unborn:
Lyn Venable of Dallas, Texas, wrote this science fiction story about a young man who need not have run. Tyndall lies listening as rockets roar and the ground trembles, fearing the ship will leave without him. Elsewhere, Bheel stands transfixed on a patio as the cry Dheb Tyn-Dall rings out and vigilant Guardians seize him.

Venable, praised as a sensitive new voice in the field, builds her tale around flight, pursuit, and a grove tied to the unborn. The story moves between panic on the ground and a departure already underway. Readers get a short, atmospheric tale of escape and capture, notable as an early appearance by a woman writer then new to science fiction.
30315-raeburn:
James L. Caw writes Raeburn, 1756 to 1823, in the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by T. Leman Hare, published in London by T. C. & E. C. Jack and in New York by Frederick A. Stokes in 1909, illustrated with eight reproductions in colour. Plate one, Lord Newton, fronts the book from the National Gallery of Scotland. A chef-d'oeuvre dating from about 1807, it represents one of the most celebrated characters ever to sit on the bench of the Court of Session.

Charles Hay, called The Mighty, lives on in Parliament House tradition for the law, paunch, whist, claret, and worth that made him famous in his day. Further plates give the children of the Patersons of Castle Huntly, Mrs. Lauzun, Mrs. Campbell of Balliemore, Professor Robison, John Tait of Harvieston and his grandson, Miss de Vismes, and Mrs. Scott Moncrieff. Caw presents the Scottish portrait painter through his sitters and his colour.
3075-the-return:
Walter de la Mare wrote The Return as a supernatural novel opening with a warning from Sir Thomas Browne against seeking roses in Attalus's garden or wholesome flowers in a venomous plantation. The book runs to twenty-three chapters, beginning in a churchyard. Arthur Lawford, a respectable man, falls asleep on a grave and wakes changed, possessed by the spirit of a dead man.

A stranger offers Lawford more of the dead man's history than the sexton knows, inviting him to a house at the foot of the hill, not half a mile distant. Lawford takes out his watch and considers the offer. The novel's horror lies in identity itself, as one man's life invades another's. It remains de la Mare's most haunting long fiction.
31621-description-of-a-new-softshell-tur:
Robert G. Webb's Description of a New Softshell Turtle from the Southeastern United States was published as University of Kansas Publications, volume eleven, number nine, pages 517 to 525, on August 14, 1959. It names and describes a softshell turtle new to science. Webb, writing for the University of Kansas at Lawrence, gives the turtle's distinguishing marks, its range in the Southeast, and the specimens on which the description rests.

Short taxonomic papers of this kind are how new species enter science: a careful description, figures, and a comparison with its nearest relatives. Webb's paper serves herpetologists working on North American turtles, and it fixes the new form's name for later study. Readers of natural history will find a precise, workmanlike piece of species description.
318-john-barleycorn:
Jack London voted on a warm California election day after several drinks, then rode home for another. John Barleycorn, published in 1913, opens in the Valley of the Moon, where London's wife Charmian asks how he voted on suffrage. His answer surprises her.

London traces his lifelong wrestle with drink, from youthful bravado to tolerant acceptance and finally to warning. Barleycorn, his name for alcohol, appears as a cunning companion and enemy. The memoir mixes confession, humor, and temperance argument. It remains a frank classic on addiction. London's memoir helped the temperance cause he came to support.
32512-historia-amoris-a-history-of-love-:
Edgar Saltus's Historia Amoris, published in New York in 1906, traces love from ancient to modern times in two parts. Part One opens by the rivers of Babylon. It moves through Solomon's curtains, Aphrodite Urania, Sappho, the age of Aspasia, and a banquet. It then turns to Roma-Amor, Antony and Cleopatra, the imperial orgy, and the end of love in the ancient world. Saltus begins with light, life, death, and fear, noting that love was absent from Eden, where Adam and Eve emerged adult.

Part Two follows the cloister and the heart, pursuivants of love, parliaments of joy, and doctors of the gay science. An apotheosis follows, then Bluebeard, the Renaissance, and love in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. A closing chapter states a law of attraction. Saltus writes in rich, aphoristic prose, treating love as history, myth, and philosophy at once.
32843-the-sun-maid-a-story-of-fort-dearb:
Evelyn Raymond tells the story of the Sun Maid at Fort Dearborn, published by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1900. Her preface calls the book an allegory: the heroine and the city of Chicago both grew from insignificant beginnings, through discouragement and seeming ruin, into courage, will, and sympathy.

Twenty-four chapters follow Kitty from sunset on the beach path, where Black Partridge reads an omen of tragedy. They pass through Indian attire, the white bow, and three gifts, to an island retreat and a cave of refuge. Later chapters bring Gaspar and Kitty to the fort, enemies seen and unseen, and faithfulness unto death. The Maid remains joyful as a girl until her century's end.
33248-milton-s-tercentenary-an-address-d:
Henry A. Beers's address, given before the Modern Language Club of Yale University on Milton's three hundredth birthday and printed in 1910, defends Milton's high place in English letters. Beers grants that rivals from Dryden to Browning are read more often and with more ease, yet holds that Milton still stands second only to Shakespeare among poets of the English tongue. He weighs the great epics against Milton's work and finds his throne unshaken.

The address is short, lucid, and made to be heard, with a speaker's eye for a telling contrast. It suits readers who want a clear statement of why Milton mattered in 1908 and why his fame had lasted through waves of new taste. Beers writes with warmth for his subject and with respect for the poets who came after him.
33345-lafcadio-hearn:
Nina H. Kennard's life of Lafcadio Hearn, copyrighted in 1912, traces the writer who bridged East and West, with letters from Hearn to his half-sister, Mrs. Atkinson. The book opens with the Hearn crest and motto, and a portrait of Hearn with his wife, setting a personal tone. Kennard follows Hearn from his early years to his fame as a voice of Japan, through his letters and her own narrative.

The life's charm lies in its intimate detail, as Hearn's own words reveal a man of keen feeling and restless mind. Kennard writes with warmth for her subject, and her use of letters gives the book a first-hand flavor. For readers who love Hearn's tales of Japan, this biography offers a fuller picture of the man behind them.
33529-the-return-of-tharn:
Howard Browne returns to a prehistoric world in this novel first serialized in Amazing Stories in late 1948. Tharn sets out to rescue his beloved Dylara, only to find the whole Cro-Magnon world arrayed against him. The story opens with Trakor, a seventeen-year-old of the tribe of Gerdak, hurrying along a jungle game trail toward his people's caves as daylight fades.

Lions, panthers, leopards, and other fierce creatures haunt the semi-tropical forest, and a slippery spear shaft can mean the difference between life and death. Browne writes fast, pulpy adventure in the lost-world manner, with young heroes, burning stockades, and savage beasts. Fans of prehistoric fantasy and golden-age science fiction magazines will enjoy its breathless pace.
3417-the-fortunes-of-oliver-horn:
Francis Hopkinson Smith sets this novel in Baltimore, opening on Kennedy Square in the late eighteen fifties. The square holds birds, trees, flowers, and old stone benches, with great magnolias scenting the air and roses climbing the railings. At its center stands the old house of Richard Horn, a noted inventor whom the book calls the man least understood.

His son Oliver grows up in that house and must make his own way as an artist and a man. Smith follows Oliver through studios, friendships, and love, against a city that is itself changing. The novel mixes a coming of age story with a portrait of old Baltimore, and it suits readers who enjoy rich settings and a hero shaped by family pride.
34173-canadian-wilds-tells-about-the-hud:
Martin Hunter wrote these tales of the Canadian wilds from forty years in the fur trade. Harding printed the book in Columbus, Ohio, in 1907. Hunter entered the Hudson's Bay Company in 1863 as a clerk and retired a commissioned officer in 1903.

His chapters teach how northern Indians hunt beaver, lynx, marten, fox, and otter. He explains outfitting, provisions, forts, and officers' rations. Stories tell of a tame seal, a bear in the water, and hungry pike. Hunter traveled by canoe and snowshoe from Labrador to Lake Superior. He traded with Montagnais, Algonquin, and Ojibway hunters and learned their methods at first hand. The book is plain bush lore from a man who lived it.
34426-the-enchanted-barn:
Grace Livingston Hill Lutz wrote The Enchanted Barn, published at Philadelphia in 1918. Its heroine is Shirley Hollister, a stenographer in a law office, who snatches a moment when her boss steps out to press her hands to her tired eyes. At home her mother lies ill in a stifling little brick house, too weak to get up for a week.

The frontispiece shows Shirley breathless at the foot of a hill, standing before a great barn. Lutz was a prolific writer of Christian romances, among them Marcia Schuyler and Phoebe Deane. Her tales pair a hard-working heroine with faith, family duty, and a kindly turn of fortune. This one turns on the barn of the title and the new life Shirley seeks for her mother and herself.
35099-the-color-line-a-brief-in-behalf-o:
The Color Line is a brief on race by William Benjamin Smith. Its full title adds that the case is made on behalf of the unborn. A sage word on ends heads the front page of the work. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen five.

Parts ask if the race or the man is the true unit of the age. One part asks in plain terms if Black folk are by nature less. Stock versus school is weighed in a long mid part of the case. Pleas from both sides, a look to years hence, and a count of heads close it. The book states the white south case for race bars in law and life.
35546-a-lowden-sabbath-morn:
A Lowden Sabbath Morn, a poem in Scots by Robert Louis Stevenson, is a short book of verses on a Sunday morning. The Lowden of the title is Lothian, the country round Edinburgh. This London edition of 1909, from Chatto and Windus, carries drawings by Boyd.

The first illustrated edition had come out in 1898, with a second run the same year. The poem opens with Sabbath bells swelling and fading over the quiet fields. Beasts and men alike know the day of rest. A ploughman dawdles half dressed, glad his week is done. A mother shoos her children out and in, fits their Sunday shoes, and slips sweets in their pouches. Then the whole house sets off on the mile to kirk.
35611-the-great-return:
The Great Return is a tale of the supernatural by Arthur Machen, author of The Bowmen, published in London in 1915. Its chapters move from rumour to miracle: odours of paradise, a secret place, and the Grail mass.

Machen opens with marvels that flash and vanish. A Reuter telegram once reported, without comment, that the Tashai Lama had ascended a holy mountain in Tibet and was transfigured. Nobody ever asked what it meant. Poltergeist stories in lonely farms get the same treatment. Machen's narrator collects such neglected wonders as his warrant. Then the tale turns to a Welsh village in wartime, where the marvellous returns in earnest and the Grail mass is celebrated again. It is Machen's wartime mysticism, written beside the angels of The Bowmen.
36254-phallic-miscellanies-facts-and-pha:
Phallic Miscellanies was privately printed in 1891 as an appendix to earlier volumes on phallism and nature worship. Its unnamed author had already written Phallicism and related works on sex worship. The book gathers facts and phases of ancient and modern sex worship, drawn chiefly from the religions of India.

The first chapters describe the linga, the sacred bull Nandi, and the rite of linga puja. They trace the growth of the Hindu pantheon, the god Siva, and the Hindu triad. Later matter compares Indian deities with those of Egypt and Greece and describes temples and ceremonies. The author says the material was gathered with great labour from sources he judged trustworthy. The book belongs to the earnest, sometimes credulous Victorian study of old religions.
36696-old-deccan-days-or-hindoo-fairy-le:
Old Deccan Days, or Hindoo fairy legends current in southern India, was collected from oral tradition by Frere and published by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1870. Sir Bartle Frere supplied an introduction and notes.

The volume frames its tales with an introduction, the collector's apology, and the narrator's own narrative. The stories were taken down from a narrator whose family had lived two generations in the Deccan. Twenty-three tales follow, among them Punchkin, Brave Seventee Bai, Truth's Triumph, Rama and Luxman, Little Surya Bai, and the Wanderings of Vicram Maharajah. Others tell how the sun, the moon, and the wind went out to dinner, how a Brahmin fared with a tiger and six judges, and how three clever men outwitted the demons.
369-the-outlaw-of-torn:
Edgar Rice Burroughs frames this medieval tale as a lost chronicle dug from a monastery in Europe. The story claims to tell of Richard, a lost prince of England, hidden and wronged in the reign of Henry III. A quarrel between king and Simon de Montfort sets the plot in motion in June 1243.

The prince grows into the visored horseman of Torn, a feared outlaw who rights wrongs by sword. Burroughs keeps the action brisk, with castle plots, chases, and duels. The book works as a bold romance of revenge and hidden birth, told in the guise of history found by chance.
37114-a-history-of-the-cries-of-london-a:
A History of the Cries of London, Ancient and Modern appeared in a second, greatly enlarged edition, with woodcuts by Thomas and John Bewick and their pupils. Its subject is the street sellers of London and the cries they used to sell their wares. Hogarth's pieman stands at the front as a first example.

The pieman, the book notes, worked in a set costume and gave a good pennyworth for a penny, while a robbery went on beside him. From prints and old accounts, the history gathers sellers of pies, fish, fruit, and more, across the centuries. It preserves a lost soundscape of the city: the daily calls that once told Londoners what was passing their doors.
37490-the-gray-phantom-s-return:
Herman Landon wrote this detective novel, published in New York in 1922. It brings back his hero the Gray Phantom, a thief turned hunter of criminals. The first chapter is named From Dying Lips, and it opens on a wet night in lower Manhattan.

Patrolman Joshua Pinto walks his beat at two in the morning, humming a joyless tune. A raw wind sweeps the corners as he turns off the Bowery into East Houston Street. Pinto's face gives nothing away, but the night is about to break open. Landon writes in the brisk pulp style of his day. Readers get a fast city mystery built on a death-bed clue.
37588-the-island-of-gold-a-sailor-s-yarn:
Gordon Stables wrote this sailor's yarn, published by Nelson in London, Edinburgh and New York. Allan Stewart drew the plates for the tale. Book one opens with a chapter called 'Two Mitherless Bairns,' in Scots words for two motherless children at the story's heart.

Ransey Tansey rises much earlier than usual on the morning his father comes home. He crawls from a box bed at the far end of a one-roomed cottage. In the corner, his little sister Babs sleeps soundly in a long basket that serves as her cradle. Ransey bends over her, thankful she still sleeps, before the day's work begins.
38044-the-ascent-of-the-matterhorn:
Edward Whymper wrote The Ascent of the Matterhorn as the record of his Alpine campaigns. John Murray issued it in London in 1880, with maps and illustrations. Whymper had gone to the Alps in 1860 as an artist, not a climber. A publisher asked him for sketches of the great peaks.

On Mont Pelvoux, a party of Englishmen failed to climb as planned. Whymper returned with friends in 1861 and reached the top. The Matterhorn then drew him by its grandeur and its name as the most sheerly unclimbable peak. Year after year he came back after each rebuff, set on finding a way up or proving none exists. The volume tells that long siege, the heart of his climbing life.
38127-from-the-oak-to-the-olive-a-plain-:
From the Oak to the Olive, a plain record of a pleasant journey, is a travel book by Julia Ward Howe. Lee and Shepard published it at Boston in 1868. Howe dedicates it to the strenuous champion of Greek liberty and of human rights. Her contents begin with preliminaries and the voyage, then Liverpool, Chester, and Lichfield.

London fills the next chapters: Saint Paul's, society, and the Channel crossing. Paris and Marseilles lead on to Rome, with Saint Peter's, Easter, works of art, and the catacombs. Naples brings excursions, Capri, and Sorrento. Florence and Venice close the Italian road before Greece. Howe, famed for the Battle Hymn of the Republic, writes as a thoughtful American abroad. She refuses to rush into the correspondent's haste, she says at the start. Her record joins churches, pictures, and peoples into a gentle, observant tour of the old world.
38321-economy-of-the-round-dairy-barn:
Wilber J Fraser wrote a farm bulletin on the worth of round dairy barns. The University of Illinois issued it at Urbana in February 1910. Fraser led dairy work at the school test station. A short summary at the front gives the whole case in ten points.

A round barn stores and spreads feed with less work, Fraser holds. Its walls stand stronger with less lumber than straight walls of like size. Stuff for a square barn costs a third to half more, by his counts. Full plans and costs for a sixty-foot round barn close the guide for builders.
38682-the-life-of-saint-columba-abbot-an:
The Life of Saint Columba tells of the abbot also called Columkille, apostle of the Picts and patron of the monastic order in Ireland. A Latin line at the head praises him as one who before God worked great wonders and praised the Lord with all his heart. The writer had already attempted lives of Saint Patrick and of Bridget. Columba is held with them as one of Erin's patrons, his name woven with theirs in Irish piety.

The first chapter treats his birth and bent, his training at Saint Finnian's, and his taking of the deacon's order. He was born about 521, of the blood of the Nialls by his father and of a famed Leinster line by his mother Aethena. A dream before his birth warned her that the child would be blessed.
38770-the-aboriginal-population-of-the-s:
The Aboriginal Population of the San Joaquin Valley, California is a lore tract by Cook. It came out in a set of such tracts from a great school press, sent in the fall of nineteen fifty-four and out the next July. Six maps stand with the text. Parts weigh the count of the first folk of that vale past the year eighteen fifty, in whole and in small tracts.

Counts are built stream by stream, from the north forks to the great lake vale of the south. A next part gives the first folk vale by vale, with the hill folk of one tribe at the close. A sum and a list of wells end the work. One first hand count put the vale past fifty thousand souls in the first years of the white come, a base the tract tests vale by vale.
38869-from-the-lakes-of-killarney-to-the:
From the Lakes of Killarney to the Golden Horn is a travel book by Henry Field, a clergyman and editor. Scribner published it in New York; the fourteenth edition is dated 1884, from a copyright of 1876. The title gives the journey's span, from Ireland's lakes to Constantinople.

Field explains the journey's origin in his opening lines. When a man's house is left desolate by the loss of the one who filled it with sunshine, the natural impulse is to wander. There is no light in the window and no fire on the hearth. So driven from home, the writer crossed the seas and passed from land to land until he had compassed the globe. The book is the record of that long grief-journey, turned by travel into a survey of Europe and the East.
39740-oriental-rugs-antique-and-modern:
Walter Hawley wrote Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern, published with eleven full-page plates. A first colour plate shows a section of the holy carpet of the mosque of Ardebil, in the Victoria and Albert Museum at South Kensington, described at pages eighty-three and eighty-four. The carpet measures thirty-four feet six inches by seventeen feet six. Its inscription, translated, says the maker has no refuge in the world other than that threshold.

Maksoud of Kashan signed it, in the year 946 of the Hegira, 1540 by our count. Vincent Robinson and Company sold it to the museum in 1892. Hawley's book teaches collectors the knots, dyes, and districts of the East.
40263-folly-as-it-flies-hit-at-by-fanny-:
Fanny Fern hit at folly in essays printed at New York in 1868. Fern gives the book to her friend Robert Bonner, editor of the New York Ledger. For fourteen years, the team of Bonner and Fern has trotted over the road at a fast pace, without a snap of the harness or a hitch of the wheels, she jokes. Plenty of oats and a skilful rein are the secret.

A discourse upon husbands opens the set, then grandmother's chat about children, women and their discontents, and women and some of their mistakes. Notes upon preachers and preaching, Bridget as she was and as she is, and a chapter on tobacco follow. Give the convicts a chance, a glance at Washington, and glimpses of camp life fill the middle. Working girls of New York and washing the baby close a sharp, warm, famous columnist's shelf.
41003-the-eye-of-istar-a-romance-of-the-:
William Le Queux wrote The Eye of Istar, a romance of the land of no return, published at New York by Frederick Stokes, with illustrations by Alfred Pearse. Le Queux, later famous for spy novels, began with such eastern romances. His preface opens in mock oriental style: peace, O reader, constant, blessed, and abundant salutations.

Of a verity, he continues, the groves of my hopes have been refreshed by cooling showers from the clouds of Allah's blessing. Behind the flowered style lies a tale of Arabia, lost cities, and a sacred gem, the eye of the goddess Istar. Le Queux had travelled in the near east as a young artist and journalist. The romance runs on disguises, deserts, and daggers in his best manner. It is early Le Queux, before the invasion novels made him a household name.
41231-the-life-and-beauties-of-fanny-fer:
Fanny Fern was one of the most loved American writers of her day, and this book pairs her life with her best pieces. It came out in Philadelphia in 1855, when her fame was at its height. The title page takes its motto from Othello: speak of me as I am.

The life tells how Fern rose from hardship to a wide and loyal readership. The beauties are chosen pieces from her work, the sharp and tender sketches that made her name. Fern wrote with wit about home life, women, and the city. Readers get both the story of her rise and a taste of the prose that won her readers.
42227-a-witch-shall-be-born:
Robert Howard wrote "A Witch Shall Be Born," a Conan story printed in Weird Tales in December 1934. Howard's barbarian hero had already made the magazine famous. This tale takes Conan to the small desert kingdom of Khauran.

Queen Taramis wakes in her dark palace to a strange glow on the wall. In the disk of light she sees a human head, and fear takes her. The tale turns on her twin sister, a witch born under a curse, who means to steal the throne. Conan serves as captain of the queen's guard when the plot strikes. Swords, sorcery, and a crucifixion scene that readers long remembered drive the story to its end.
42761-fables-and-fabulists-ancient-and-m:
Thomas Newbigging wrote Fables and Fabulists, Ancient and Modern, shown here in a cheap edition printed in London in 1896. Newbigging had written a history of the Forest of Rossendale. A front picture shows Mercury giving the young Aesop the gift of the fable, and verses by Andrew Lang praise the old storyteller.

The opening chapters define the fable, set out its traits, and weigh the moral each tale carries. Newbigging shows how fabulists acted as critics of their times and what lessons their beasts and birds taught. He then moves through the great makers, starting with Aesop. The book serves readers who want both the tales themselves and a clear account of why short animal stories have lasted so long.
42894-the-shadow-of-victory-a-romance-of:
The Shadow of Victory, a romance of Fort Dearborn by Myrtle Reed, appeared in 1903. Putnam published it at New York and London in September of that year. A plate shows an arrow singing past a girl on horseback in flight. The prophecy opens the contents as chapter one of the tale.

New acquaintances and the second in command follow in the contents list. Ronald views of marriage fills the fourth chapter of the romance. The first flower of spring stands further down the chapter roll shown. Old Chicago as a frontier fort in 1812 gives the tale its ground and danger. Reed sweet style dresses a massacre shadowed love story in this early novel.
43437-memoirs-of-miss-sidney-biddulph-ex:
Frances Sheridan's Memoirs of Miss Sidney Bidulph was drawn, its title page says, from the heroine's own journal and now first published. The editor inscribes the work to the author of Clarissa and Sir Charles Grandison, as a tribute where goodness and genius unite in one person. The hosted text runs through three volumes, and a supplement, Cecilia's narrative, continues a second journal kept by Arnold.

The story opens on the heroine's mother, Catharine Sidney Bidulph, and the family she heads. Her eldest son would later be Sir George Bidulph, the estate was not large, and Miss Bidulph's portion stood at four thousand pounds. At the time, the narrative dryly notes, that fortune was far from contemptible.
43927-a-sermon-delivered-before-his-exce:
Election Sermon of eighteen twenty eight was preached by James Walker in Massachusetts. Dutton and Wentworth, printers to the state, issued it at Boston that year. Walker spoke before Governor Levi Lincoln and both houses of the legislature. The day was the general election day, May twenty eighth, in Boston.

The House voted thanks to Walker and asked a copy for the press. His text is from Exodus, on choosing able men who fear God. Walker warns he must be brief and tied to the day at hand. No long learned talk suits an audience come for public business, he says. Readers get a civic sermon on the traits fit for rulers.
44182-the-red-tavern:
C R Macauley wrote The Red Tavern, a tale of knights and intrigue published in New York and London in 1914. A front plate shows an armed man asking a host for peace and provender for a wayfaring knight, and that old-world tone runs through the whole book.

A warrant against Douglas sets young Sir Richard on the road to Castle Yewe, with a night at the Red Tavern early in his ride. Chapters pile up incident: a wolf-hound, an ambush, a duel, and an escape. Sir Richard delivers the king's warrant, jousts with Bull Bengough, and rescues a maiden. A vision in the forest and a spell playing king close the plot, before the tavern meets its end. The prose mimics old chronicle speech, and fans of costume romance get a full feast of it.
45006-general-smith-s-views-of-the-power:
Joseph Smith set out his thoughts on the might and the course of the state in this tract. It was printed at Nauvoo, Illinois, by John Taylor in 1844. Born in a land of the free, the tract opens. Its air is free of the taint of wild climes. The author feels a two-fold care for the joy of all men, in time and in the life to come.

His thoughts, like those of Daniel, have long put him in pain, he says. He has viewed the state of men through the world. Most of all he has viewed it in this proud realm. There the great scroll of the land holds truths to be plain in them. All men are made the same, as the tract starts to quote.
49286-custer-s-last-shot-or-the-boy-trai:
Custer's Last Shot; or, The Boy Trailer of the Little Horn is a dime novel by Col J M Travers. Frank Tousey published it in New York on July 11, 1883. It is number 565 of the Five Cent Wide Awake Library. The price was 5 cents, complete in the number. Its subtitle calls it a romance of the terrible ride to death. Sixteen chapters carry the campaign.

The yellow-haired cavalry chief opens on the war trail. Sitting Bull's gang of red marauders opposes him. The reckless gallop and brave Custer's last shot come by chapter four. How the command paid for immortality follows. Reno's rifle-pits on the river bluffs mark the disaster's edge. The boy trailer goes to work in chapter fourteen. The opening scene sets the tone. A buckskin hunter holds his rifle on chief Yellow Hawk, and catechises him in frontier dialect.
49937-motor-matt-s-defiance-or-around-th:
Motor Matt's Defiance, or Around the Horn, is number nineteen of Motor Stories, dated July the third, nineteen nine, and sold for five cents. Street and Smith of New York issued the weekly tale of motor thrills. Motor Matt is a lad at home with every kind of motor, known as Mile-a-minute Matt for his daring races. His nerve, the cast list says, carries him through straits that would daunt most youths.

His mates are Carl Pretzel, a stout and merry German boy, and Dick Ferral, a young sea dog from Canada. An ensign named Glennie rides for the United States government on a long trip round South America. Foes include escaped convicts from Punta Arenas and a strange ship that sails under many flags. Chapter heads promise treachery, a dive for liberty, and a run north.
50742-the-story-of-beowulf-translated-fr:
Ernest Kirtlan turned the Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf into modern English prose for this Crowell edition. Kirtlan had earlier translated 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight' into English as well. Long notes sit in an appendix, and the reader is urged to check them where footnotes point, for a clearer grasp of people and events.

The introduction stresses a sense of destiny in the poem. Life in Beowulf, Kirtlan writes, is a grave thing, with none of the glad passion for beauty found in Celtic tales. Mist, angry seas and massive, threatening scenery match that sombre view of the Teutonic world.
52256-the-lead-pencil-manufactory-of-a-w:
The Lead Pencil Manufactory of A W Faber tells one hundred years of a pencil house. The Stein works near Nürnberg marked its first century in eighteen hundred sixty one. The owner gave the sketch to his patrons and trade friends. Moss and Company of Philadelphia sold the Siberian line in America.

Faber pencils came in grades from soft black to extra hard. Six B marks the softest, and six H the hardest point. Cards of ten held one of each grade for the buyer’s desk. Artists’ patent pencils took loose leads of any grade. Moss stocked drawing tools and tracing cloth at its Chestnut Street shop. The sketch calls the pencil a new age tool of great worth. Old Rome knew no such aid for art or study, it notes. Lead in name alone ties the black core to the grey metal.
52346-the-story-of-old-fort-dearborn:
J Seymour Currey wrote The Story of Old Fort Dearborn, a book put out at Chicago in 1912. Eleven plates fill the work. Currey gave the book to Nelly Kinzie Gordon. A note on Henry Dearborn tells of his long life in arms and in high posts.

The first word states that there were two forts of that name on the site. The first rose in 1803 and held a troop of the United States. It was razed by the tribes just past the grim killings of 1812. A second fort rose on the same ground in 1816. It served in spans, with gaps when peace held firm. The site had borne the name Chekagou on a French map of 1684. The book ties the fort to the birth of the town that grew past it.
53446-the-mare-chale-catherine-booth-cli:
James Strahan, a minister and writer on Hebrew thought, wrote this life of Catherine Booth-Clibborn, the Maréchale, published in 1914. The catalog title is her name in brackets. She was a daughter of William and Catherine Booth, founders of the Salvation Army, and she carried the Army into France and Switzerland as its marshal, the French title the book bears.

Strahan's preface says the book came of a brief visit she paid her daughter and himself that spring. She was daily persuaded, not so much to talk of the past as to live parts of her life over again, rising from the table to act her stories out. The life is told from that living memory. It honors a preacher of fire.
55920-journal-of-a-tour-in-the-years-182:
Tobin, a young doctor, kept a journal of a tour made with the great chemist Humphry Davy in 1828 and 1829. Orr of London published it in 1832. A preface says the pages were meant at first only for his family and close friends.

Davy's health was broken, and he sought its mending in travel through Styria, Carniola, and Italy. He asked Tobin's mother, then at Heidelberg, to let her son go as his companion and helper. She gave up the young man's studies without a pause. Tobin warns that Davy often wished to be alone, ate by himself, and rode for hours without a word. Pain made his moods shift fast. Yet his spirit, the young man says, stayed radiant and strong.
56205-voyager-1-encounters-saturn:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration issued this picture book on the Voyager 1 flight past Saturn, dated December 1980. Robert A Frosch, the head of the agency, signed the front matter. The cover shows Saturn with two moons, Tethys and Dione, shot on November 3, 1980, from thirteen million kilometres away. Tethys casts its shadow on the cloud tops.

Voyager 1 had left Cape Canaveral on September 5, 1977, bound for Jupiter, Saturn, and beyond. Chapters treat the planet, its rings, and its moons, then sum up the mission and its tools. Each photo gives its date and the craft's range. New moons, Titan, and the magnetosphere stand out in the results list.
56233-the-purple-fern:
Fergus Hume wrote a mystery tale whose name is a fern of odd hue. The book came out in London in 1907. Hume wrote The Mystery of a Hansom Cab with great fame. A man in grey starts the tale, and a bold act comes next. Twins, a riddle, and a vicar fill the first parts.

A find, a cure man's tale, and a quest in court build the knot. A chance hiss, a dog, and trade acts fill the mid arc. New times, Prudence, and the vicar's own woes mark the turns. A strange note, a call back, and a shock close the list. Zara the Butterfly and proof in full end the hunt. Crime fans get Hume's hand.
56248-persian-literature-ancient-and-mod:
Elizabeth Reed wrote Persian Literature, Ancient and Modern, after a like book on Hindu letters. Griggs of Chicago put it out for general readers in the West. Reed held seats in learned groups at home and abroad, and wrote to open Eastern classics to plain folk.

Her survey runs from old Persian epic and sacred verse to later poets and prose. A famed Shah Namah page fronts the book in copy. Reed gives plots, lives, and short samples in clear English dress. She writes as a guide, not a critic, and keeps hard names light. The book shows how keen the West then was to read Persia's store of song.
57302-spirits-do-return:
Ida Belle White wrote Spirits Do Return, issued in Kansas City in nineteen fifteen. Her own White Publishing Company brought it out. The title page makes a bold claim in plain type: inspired by Samuel L Clemens, Mark Twain. Twain had died five years before the book appeared.

White holds that the dead return and speak to the living. A famed humorist's spirit stands as her chief witness. Spiritualism filled many American parlours in those years, and the war soon filled more. Books like this one promised grieving readers a voice from the other side. Whether the reader believes or not, the volume is a period piece. It shows how Twain's fame followed him past the grave.
57587-the-elves-of-mount-fern:
The Elves of Mount Fern is a fairy story book by Katherine Creighton, published at Philadelphia in nineteen twenty two. Dorrance issued it, and Creighton had written nature songs and sketches before. She dedicates the book to lovers of fairies everywhere in the world. Five chapters tell of one company of elves in the giant world.

Elves, the tale says, are the dearest and most mischievous of little people. They live in Elfland, found in every corner of the globe at once. By night they dance on dewy lawns and visit friends among men unseen. One company leaves its forest glade for a season in a stone wall. The wall guards Doctor Templeton's garden, and its lazy gardener drops stones from it. A lawn party, a ball, and a birthday fill the middle chapters. The king of the elves pays Mount Fern a visit at the last.
58653-the-revealing-pattern:
Alvin Heiner wrote The Revealing Pattern, a science fiction tale printed in Worlds of If in May 1952. The head note gives the hook in one line, that the Reamer mansion was on trial and announced its own verdict of guilty. A house that judges is a strange start, and Heiner builds the mystery from there.

The tale opens on a man easily smiled at, a small birdlike fellow with an umbrella and a pink face. He wears the look of a man with happy secrets about to be revealed. Heiner mixes that mild figure with a haunted or thinking house. Readers get a compact puzzle tale, where a pattern hidden in events points to the truth.
58806-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Frances Hodgson Burnett. The file lists her books held in the Gutenberg set. Each entry then gives that book’s own table of contents. Titles run from The Secret Garden to The Head of the House of Coombe.

A reader can scan the shape of each tale before opening it. The Secret Garden shows chapters on Mary, the robin, and the locked garden. A Little Princess lists Sara, the attic, and the Indian gentleman. Short tales and plays sit beside the long novels. The index suits readers who want to pick a Burnett book by its parts. It also helps track which texts the project holds.
59345-slow-burn:
Henry Still wrote Slow Burn, a science fiction tale printed in the October 1955 issue of Worlds of If. Its head note says the problems of space were trouble enough without the opinions and treachery of Senator McKelvie, who put the fat into the fire. Kevin Morrow commands a space station and has only to get it out. He gulps the last of his coffee and stares through the plastic port at the stars and the swinging curve of the station.

Four space-suited tugmen float outside the rim, and the black and white moonship tugs at her mooring lines, keen to be off. Bert Alexander radios quiet orders to the tugmen. McKelvie, who has been after their hide since the appropriation, is coming up to kibitz on the biggest day of the year. Still builds his tale on station routine and political spite.
59825-a-case-of-sunburn:
Charles L Fontenay plants a spy hunt in A Case of Sunburn, from Worlds of If Science Fiction in April 1957. The blurb sets the stakes: in the past year the Martian rebels have been pushed back to the wall, and all that is left to them is Plan Blue. What Plan Blue is, the tale means to show.

Jonner waits at a rendezvous above Syrtis Major with four men, as Sir Stanrich promised. Then a fifth groundcar swings in with a sixth man, and every credential looks alike. One of them must be a Marscorp spy, and there is no time to check.
60090-the-dim-lantern:
Temple Bailey wrote this novel, copyrighted in 1922 and issued the next year by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia. Coles Phillips drew the pictures, and the front one shows the heroine in an orange cloak shining through mist like a lamp. The heroine is Jane, and the chapters follow her from a singer's opening scene through knitting, waiting, and a spell as an ugly duckling.

Bailey was a beloved writer of gentle romances, and The Dim Lantern is her kind of story: a plain girl with a warm heart, set against brighter and colder people. A famished pilgrim and a call to stay in the field give the tale its turns. The lantern of the title is Jane herself, a small light in a foggy world.
60364-the-german-fury-in-belgium-experie:
L Mokveld, war reporter for De Tijd, wrote The German Fury in Belgium, turned into English by C Thieme. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book in nineteen seventeen. Mokveld spent four months with the German army in Belgium.

He admits he had no clear idea how a modern war would run when he was sent. Chapters follow the road to Liège, the ruin of Visé, and the destruction of Louvain. Dinant's ruin and the siege of Antwerp come later. A chapter treats the ill-treatment of British wounded, and the last stands on the Yser. The contents call the burning of Visé a planned crime. First-hand witness drives the book.
60695-the-night-of-hoggy-darn:
McKenna wrote The Night of Hoggy Darn, a science fiction story first printed in Worlds of If in December 1958. The author had earlier written The Fishdollar Affair, set in the same grim frontier world of New Cornwall. The story follows Flinter Cole, a young ecologist traveling to a hermit planet.

Cole rides the space freighter Gorbals, the only ship that calls at New Cornwall twice a year. Nothing has been published about the planet for five hundred years, which leaves him with no data for his doctoral field trial. The crew warns him that the New Cornish are huge, rough men who greet curious strangers with hard looks. Cole has six months to survey the planet and report. The tale mixes frontier grit with a scholar's unease.
61434-mightiest-qorn:
Keith Laumer wrote Mightiest Qorn, a science fiction story printed in Worlds of If in July 1963. Ambassador Nitworth glares across his nine-foot platinum desk and asks his staff about the Qornt. His staff, including the bumbling Magnan, knows nothing.

The Qornt were a warlike race who vanished two hundred years ago. Now they hold the inner planet of the system, on land the ambassador calls Terran territory. The Qornt despise all humans, the blurb says, except one. Laumer's Retief-style world of pompous diplomats and sly aliens drives the comedy. Short, dry, and quick, the story shows his diplomatic service farce at its best.
616-prayers-written-at-vailima-and-a-low:
Robert Louis Stevenson writes family prayers for his Samoan household in this small volume, with an introduction by his wife. Evening prayer and hymns closed each Samoan day, and Stevenson, three miles above Apia at Vailima, joined the rite with thanks for home, food, friends, and work. Prayers for success, grace, rain, friends, and renewal fill the pages.

A Lowden Sabbath Morn, a Scots poem, follows the prayers. Stevenson's words are plain, warm, and direct, asking for courage, gaiety, and a quiet mind. The book charms as a glimpse of the writer at home, where faith was a daily habit, not a Sunday show.
61759-cave-dwellers-of-saturn:
Cave Dwellers of Saturn, a science fiction story by John Wiggin, was printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1939. Across Earth's bright civilization lie the shadows of globe headed dwarfs from Mars, its headnote says. One lone Earth ship dares the blockade. It risks the planetoid peril to find Earth's life element on Saturn of the ten terrible rings.

The story opens on a crisp morning in Copia, a vast city whose avenues run like wheel spokes to Government City. A sentry at the north gate watches a man circle down through the air. Soon the soldier Dynamon stands before Argallum, commander in chief of the armies of the world. Wiggin writes in the bold pulp manner, with ray age cities, alien foes, and a desperate voyage. The tale sends its heroes past Mars to the caves of Saturn on a mission for Earth's survival.
62261-planet-of-no-return:
Peacock's Planet of No Return ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1942, a space-patrol tale set on Venus. Patrolmen Kerry Blane and Splinter Wood fly under plain orders: destroy the Thing of Venus.

The two men bicker from the first page, the grizzled Blane scorning Wood's vitamin pills and warnings about the space bends. Wrecked on the water-world of Venus, they find their weapons useless against the Thing they were sent to kill. The story runs on the clash between the old pilot and the young one as much as on the planet itself. It is a fair sample of the rough, fast pulp science fiction of its years.
62306-novelties-things-made-with-aunt-ly:
Novelties and Things Made with Aunt Lydias Heavy Rug Yarn is a pattern book from a thread house of Stamford. It sold for a few cents as one of a star book set, with the house mark on its first page. Each plan gives the stuffs, hook size, and stitch counts the work calls for.

The first plan in the copy at hand is a tank dress in three sizes, small, mid, and large. It names the count of skeins in each hue the dress needs, and the hook size to use, or any hook that gives the set gauge. Widths for front and back at the arm line are given for each size. The back is then worked row by row, with hue shifts marked as the work grows.
62487-make-it-with-aunt-lydia-s-heavy-ru:
Make It with Aunt Lydia's Heavy Rug Yarn is Star Book number 207, a pattern booklet from the American Thread Company of Stamford, Connecticut. It sold for thirty-five cents. Its cover promises flowers, pillows, toys, and rugs, made by knit, crochet, and fringe with the firm's heavy rug yarn.

The first pattern is an embroidered pillow, worked in moss and cerise yarn with yellow cotton, over shredded foam rubber with a lining and button molds. Each pattern lists the skeins, hooks, and gauge needed, then walks the maker row by row and round by round. Charts of stitch counts keep the shapes true. It is mid-century American craft print, brisk and exact.
63028-reinstern:
Reinstern, by Eloise Richberg, was published in Cincinnati in 1900. A front plate shows a dark-eyed lad and a fair-haired lass hand in hand. The contents pair Reinstern with a second piece, Love's Destiny. The tale opens on a train rushing for hours over yellow-brown plains.

The narrator, a weary woman traveler, watches willow-fringed streams, water tanks, and dreary cabins pass. Drear folk squat by the roadside for a glimpse of the train. From dull window gazing she sinks into anxious thoughts of loved ones left behind, their health and even lives in doubt. A crash and lurch stop the train, and all are called out onto a wide springy place. Richberg mixes prairie travel with romance.
63321-mr-waddy-s-return:
Theodore Winthrop wrote Mr Waddy's Return, but he did not live to revise the draft. Henry Holt and Company issued it in New York in 1904, edited by Burton Stevenson. Winthrop's sister kept the manuscript for years and judged it too good to let die. The tale opens with an unrecorded episode in the voyage of the Mayflower.

The Waddy family of Dullish Court leads down to the hero. He reaches Halifax and meets a misadventure, then a wreck and a rescue follow. Miss Sullivan, a lady of fortune, braves a storm at sea. Later, a rich returned nabob charms a fashionable watering place. Horace Belden plots villainies old and new until he reaches the end of his rope. Race, picnic, and birthday party fill the lighter chapters.
63697-space-lane-of-no-return:
Space Lane of No Return is a science fiction story by George A Whittington, taken from Planet Stories for summer 1946. A blurb says the lane keeping crews were bored with dull duty and wanted danger. Then the swift blaze of the void found them, and they were blasted toward nothing.

Nord Holber tells himself that asteroid fishing is no job for men who joined the Inter Planetary Patrol for distant frontiers. His two man ship hangs less than twenty degrees off the ecliptic, with hard starlight on its maroon plastic hull. Below, asteroids rush like the ghosts of shattered planets. Small fragments dance above them, the hazard that forces liners to arc high above the Belt. Holber, fresh from Federation University, faces his first true peril. Space tale fans get patrol duty turned deadly.
63899-the-giants-return:
Robert Abernathy wrote this science fiction story, printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1949. The starship Quest Three slows toward a yellow sun after a long search. Its crew has passed giant stars and nebulae and found world after world with no life. Children aboard were born in the ship and have never seen a planet.

Now hope rises as a sun like Earth's own grows near. The opening blurb warns that Earth will meet the returning giants with corrosive fire, fearing the Old Ones. Yet the blurb adds that the giants are clever despite their size. The tale sets up a clash between a wary Earth and travelers coming home after ages away.
64530-spacemen-are-born:
Spacemen Are Born is a short star tale by Bolling Branham from Planet Stories of May nineteen fifty two. Trase Barnes, a desk chief of Air Lines, bets he can shoot the rings of Saturn and live. All know space men are born, not made, the tag line warns. An old moon man tells the tale with ache for the far sky road. Space songs and ring tales stir that ache in his bones each day.

Ships coast in with slack jets and cut in past the outer ring rim. On the fourth day they pass twixt the great ring and the thin crape ring. Saturn gold bulk with grape hue streaks fills the sky in that gap. Trase was born on the Moon in a wire room of the line post. Fake pull of weight helped his blood run at his first breath.
64864-newcom-tavern:
Newcom Tavern tells the story of Dayton's first famed inn and the men who opened the Ohio country. Colonel George Newcom, shown in an 1852 portrait at age eighty-one, still looks flinty in the plate. His first log cabin later served as a kitchen and now stands in Carillon Park.

The tale starts with scouts who crossed the Alleghenies and praised the Miami lands back East. Rich soil, game, and grass drew settlers west in the late 1700s. Newcom's tavern grew with the town into a hub of trade and talk. This local history keeps a frontier crossroads alive in print.
65316-head-gear-antique-and-modern:
Head-Gear, Antique and Modern, from 1879, comes from Wadleigh's fashionable millinery and cap rooms on Washington Street in Boston. The shop kept untrimmed chip and straw hats and bonnets on hand at all times. The book blends trade lists with a look at hats and caps across the ages, as its title promises.

Pages show the styles a Boston buyer could order, trim, and wear in the late 1870s. Old forms sit beside new ones, so a reader can trace how caps, bonnets, and hats changed shape. For students of dress, the book is a shop window into its day, with prices, shapes, and the language of the hat trade kept plain.
65623-a-short-treatise-on-boots-and-shoe:
Walter Goater's Short Treatise on Boots and Shoes, Ancient and Modern, was presented by Slater of Broadway, New York. Eleven illustrations accompany the text. Footwear begins, Goater says, as soles fastened by thongs between the toes and round the ankle. Such sandals served the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans. Paintings on the walls of Thebes show shoemaking as a distinct, lucrative trade under Thothmes the Third, fifteen hundred years before Christ.

Egyptian priests wore sandals of palm and papyrus leaves; specimens survive in the British Museum. Rhodope, the Cinderella of the Nile, lost such a sandal to an eagle, and the king who received it made her queen. Greek and Roman men long went barefoot by training, then magistrates took red shoes and soldiers knee-high boots. Women's shoes were white, senators' black, magistrates' red. Leather, Goater notes, has been the chief material throughout.
65624-a-short-treatise-on-head-wear-anci:
A Short Treatise on Head Wear, Ancient and Modern, with rights held from eighteen eighty-five, traces how men have covered the head through the ages. Drawings by Goater show the forms in rows of figures. Man, the book says, took the thick hair nature gave him as a hint to cover his head all the more. The hat sits on top of all dress, so it drew plumes, jewels, and bands of gold.

Crowns mark kings, a red hat marks a cardinal, and a cap with bells marks a court fool. Stuffs of all kinds, bird plumes, wool, fur, and gems have gone into hats. Felt hats are the oldest kind, the book says, while silk hats are quite new. A tale credits Saint Clement with the find of felting on a charity walk.
65629-the-boy-ranger-or-the-heiress-of-t:
Boy Ranger is a dime novel by Oll Coomes of the Golden Horn heiress. Beadle and Adams of New York issued it in eighteen seventy four. Coomes also wrote Hawkeye Harry, the Young Trapper Ranger, for Beadle. Seventeen chapters run from Rollo the Ranger to A Revelation at end.

The halter of justice, a proposed meeting, and an attack open the drama. Old Tumult to the rescue and outwitted foes fill the next short chapters. A betrothal, a desperate conflict, and the pipe of peace follow in turn. A tragedy at the lake and a villain defeated build the close acts. Rollo rides at breakneck speed toward Clontarf Post as it opens.
66477-stern:
Stern is a novel by Bruce Jay Friedman, issued at New York in 1962 and here in its second printing. Friedman dedicates it to his darling Ginger. A prologue opens on a day in early summer. It seemed, almost by a wonder, that Stern would not have to sell his house and move away after all, the first lines say.

Small blossoms had come out on one of the black and spotted trees of what Stern called his cancer garden. There was talk of a child in the neighbourhood for his son to play with. His son, a lonely boy, sat each day in the middle of the lawn sucking on blankets. Stern had also found a swift new shortcut across the estate, cutting ten minutes off his walk to the train. Giant gray dogs beyond a fence still waited to take his wrists in their mouths.
66773-two-years-among-new-guinea-canniba:
Pratt, a naturalist and fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, published Two Years Among New Guinea Cannibals in 1906. Fifty four pictures and a map fill the book, and his son Henry added notes and the science results at the back. A frontispiece shows two New Guinea dandies of Dinawa, with laced waists and polished shell nose ornaments. Pratt calls the island the second largest in the world, and the last to guard its secrets.

His contents boast of riches: seven hundred seventy known kinds of birds, and insects beyond count. Travel there meant razor ridges in endless lines and transport as the chief bugbear. The second chapter confesses disappointments in the Dutch end of the island, where a fierce people, the Tugeri, raided with bamboo knives and made science unsafe beyond the post. Pratt writes as a collector who walked where maps were blank.
67106-youth-vol-i-no-7-september-1902-an:
Youth was an illustrated monthly journal for boys and girls from the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia, and this is its September 1902 number, the seventh of its first volume.
