A picture of the Penn Cottage leads the contents. Two serial stories run in the number: one with Washington at Valley Forge, and one called A Daughter of the Forest.

Short pieces fill the rest: a trip to the Florida Everglades, Audubon at Bird Rock, and a note on flowerless plants. A poem on the whip-poor-will and a page of wood folk talk add the outdoor note. Puzzles, parlor magic, and the editor's own page close the number. It is a well stuffed magazine for a 1902 schoolchild.
67309-elsie-s-friends-at-woodburn:
Martha Finley wrote Elsie's Friends at Woodburn as one of her long Elsie series. Dodd, Mead and Company held it under copyright in 1887. The book stands late in the list of Elsie tales, after Elsie's Kith and Kin. Captain Raymond and his kin at Woodburn carry much of the story.

Snow and sleet open the book at Christmas time. Max Raymond takes Evelyn Leland by carriage from Woodburn to the Oaks. Talk turns to cold winters and old homes in the North. Family visits, faith, and courtship shape the chapters that follow. Finley writes for readers who had followed Elsie from childhood, and who now watch the next generation grow up in the same circle.
70338-paper-paper-making-ancient-and-mod:
Herring, a paper maker, published this history and manual of his trade with Longman at London in 1855, with an introduction by Croly. He dedicates it to Sir Francis Graham Moon, the lord mayor. The first chapter asks how men recorded events before paper: stones, bricks, metals, skins, tablets, leaves, and bark. Egyptian papyrus follows, from which paper took its name, and the art travels into Europe.

Whatman and the Fourdrinier machine bring the story to modern manufacture. The second chapter works through the materials and the processes: comminution, washing, bleaching, sizing, and the cutting machine. Watermarks get their due, down to Ireland's fabrication of the Shakespeare manuscripts and the light-and-shade marks of the new bank note. Bleaching anecdotes, ultramarine, and the excise duty on paper close the third chapter. The book began as lectures, and keeps a lecturer's pride: the trade explained by a man of the trade.
70721-the-cairn:
The Cairn is a gift book of short pieces, prose and verse, gathered from many hands. George Bell of London published it in eighteen forty-six. The woman who built it signs herself only as a soldier's daughter. She raised her cairn, a heap of stones, from the work of friends now dead and from her own reading.

Short pieces treat joy and sorrow, a mother's love, and tales of great names like Sir Walter Raleigh. Others muse on the grave yard at Pisa, pride, want, and faith. Most run a page or two, fit for an idle hour. The maker hopes the book can do no harm and may give some cheer. It shows the taste of its age for brief, grave, tender reading.
70852-the-chinese-lantern:
Chinese Lantern is a play in verse and prose by Laurence Housman. Sidgwick published it in London in the year 1908. A note says the play has been publicly performed in England. Rights stand reserved, with entry at the Library of Congress in Washington. Master Olangtsi, a master of arts, heads the list of persons.

His wife is called Mrs Back of the House in that list. Seven students, apprentices, and craftsmen bear comic rhyming names in turn. A Chinese Jew rag and bone merchant and his brother join the cast. A bottle washer drudge and a Korean slave girl fill low places. Act one sets a Chinese studio with windowed walls of paper.
71565-the-men-return:
The Men Return is a science fiction story by Jack Vance. It appeared in Infinity in July 1957, with illustrations by Engle. The editors gave it their Infinity-plus mark of unusual merit. They warned that readers would love it tremendously or hate it violently. An epigraph shows Alpha kneading air, blue liquid, and rock together. The story's world is one where nature's laws have come loose.

The Relict comes furtively down a crag. He is a shambling, gaunt creature with tortured eyes. He hides behind panels of dark air and passing shadows. Below him a family of grey objects melts from spheres to pyramids to tesseracts. Plants grow on floating lumps of water or around cores of hard black gas. A pair of Organisms plays on the plain, resembling men. The Relict hopes to kill one for food. Duration itself, the narrator notes, has lost all reality.
71815-outside-saturn:
Robert Ernest Gilbert wrote Outside Saturn, a science fiction story printed in Infinity in January 1958, with pictures by Richard Kluga. The head note sets the scene in slang: gangsters were out of date, and the ice sweeper was an unlikely thing to steal. But Vicenzo was a streak, so what else could Henry do?

The story opens in space, where Aziz rips the radio from Henry's suit and reseals the panel with care. Vicenzo cleverly shorts Henry's drive tube while the talk goes on. Henry, a kid being set adrift, barely gets a word in. Gilbert writes space crime in the tough talk of the pulps. The tale mixes future gear with old fashioned double cross.
72269-pattern:
Robert Rohrer wrote Pattern, a science fiction story printed in Amazing Stories in October 1962. Its beings are not flesh at all but living patterns of electric impulse in the void of space. Rahll, the hero, floats dying at the start, aware that he will soon scatter into aimless patterning with no mind or unity. His kind once lived joined in one Great Pattern, a vast web of thought.

They had given each other life and kept their powers fresh for ages of peace. Then came the Cataclysm, when some impulses tired of the old pattern and sought a new one, and the two sides broke the whole apart. Rahll alone escaped, badly hurt, and floated in darkness for thousands of years, waiting for a sign of another of his kind. The head note poses its hard choice: fighting fire with fire.
72468-the-life-of-john-worth-kern:
Claude Bowers wrote The Life of John Worth Kern, printed at Indianapolis in 1918 by the Hollenbeck Press. A portrait shows Kern in 1913, at the height of his power in the Senate. Bowers gave the book to the two sons of Kern, and he prints a saying of the senator at the front.

Kern said it is fine to feel one's boy may become a great man, but he would rather his boys be good without being great than great without being good. The first chapter treats childhood and early years. Bowers, a rising Indiana writer, tells the life of a party leader who steered the Senate in the Wilson years. Readers get warm political biography.
73476-the-subaltern:
G R Gleig wrote The Subaltern, first published in Blackwood's Magazine and revised for this library edition of eighteen seventy-two. Gleig had risen to chaplain-general of Her Majesty's forces. His preface looks back across forty-six years since the tale was written. The events themselves lay near sixty years in the past.

Four great powers stood at deadly strife when the tale opens. Gleig had served as a young officer, a subaltern, in that war against France. His book tells a young man's campaign life from the inside. Blackwood and Sons issued the revised text in Edinburgh and London. It stands among the best loved soldier memoirs of the Peninsular War.
73619-one-good-turn:
Bertrand W Sinclair tells a tale of the woods of the great Northwest, where a camp meeting sets a long chain in motion. Bill Goodrich waits in camp for his hunting partner, who has gone out for tobacco and food. A stranger with a burro and a carbine comes into the firelight instead, and Goodrich shares his meal and his fire.

The opening blurb warns that a hidden tragedy lies behind the quiet woods, with strange results years later. The stranger is hunting work at a logging camp on Slate Creek, not game. What passes between the two men at that fire shapes the rest of the story and the lives it touches.
75020-an-sthetics-antient-and-modern:
Anaesthetics Antient and Modern is an historical sketch of anaesthesia published by Burroughs Wellcome and Company of London, the drug firm. Pictures show an operation on the eye from a thirteenth-century manuscript and a surgeon at work from a seventeenth-century woodcut. The index opens with the dawn of anaesthesia and early Egyptian anaesthetics, then anaesthesia in Roman times, an antient Chinese anaesthetic, and anaesthesia in romance and in the antient poets.

Later entries reach local anaesthesia in old times and chloroform. The little book was a trade gift that doubled as scholarship, tracing how mankind dulled pain from poppy and mandrake to ether and chloroform. It serves historians of surgery well.
75710-by-way-of-cape-horn:
By Way of Cape Horn, by Paul Eve Stevenson, tells of four months in a Yankee clipper, the Hosea Higgins, on a voyage around the Horn. Stevenson had already sailed to India with his wife and written A Deep- Water Voyage. Restlessness took them to sea again. His wife searched the Herald's ship news each morning for deep-water vessels, and soon they signed on for the long passage. Photographs taken by the author fill the book, from the course chart to a fifty-foot Cape Horn graybeard.

The copyright is 1898 and the edition here is the fourth, printed in 1908. Stevenson writes as a gentleman passenger who worked and watched, recording sail drill, storms, and ship routine. The clipper age was ending when he sailed, and the book preserves its daily life from inside the cabin.
76562-the-children-of-old-park-s-tavern:
Frances Humphrey wrote a tale for the young set on the South Shore. The book came out in New York in 1886. Humphrey wrote Dean Stanley with the Children as well. Dolly goes to a meeting in the first part of the tale. Marshes and the home of Webster set the old shore scene.

Skatta, a pet or friend of the house, threads the tale. A match in the old muster field and the death of Gaston stir it. A hid room, a school chief, and a first fight fill the mid parts. Skatta is lost, and Ned rides to the rescue in time. Thanks days, a gold gown, and a wed rite close it.
77231-the-trail-of-the-golden-horn:
Cody wrote a tale of the Yukon that Doran copyrighted in 1923, sold in Toronto by McClelland and Stewart. Chapter one is named The Smokeless Cabin. Hugo, a trapper, halts on a steep hill in the hard cold and rubs the frost from his eyelids. Below him, close to the river, stands a small cabin among young firs. No smoke rises from its pipe.

Bill Haines has not moved in the night, Hugo is sure. Something must be wrong. The land round is one vast waste of snow, dark woods, and high peaks. The river lies frozen from bank to bank, save where swift water breathes vapour into the air. Hugo hates that river and holds it a treacherous demon, ever open for new prey. Had Bill slipped while drawing water? Thirty more chapters of storm, loss, rescue, and sin follow on the trail.
78566-a-president-is-born:
President Is Born is a novel by Fannie Hurst, published by Harper in 1928. Eight printings ran through December 1927 alone before the 1928 title date. Hurst dedicates the book to the memory of Henry Stephen Schuyler in front. Thanks go to the Schuyler family and to Senator Bettina Schuyler Sterling for access.

Family papers and privilege of access suggest a life built on a real political house. A president making, from birth to ambition, is the promised arc of the title. Hurst was among the best paid American story writers of her decade. Her novel gives the political dynasty tale a woman novelist eye.
78762-van-zorn:
Edwin Arlington Robinson's Van Zorn, a comedy in three acts, was published by Macmillan at New York in September 1914, with all acting rights reserved by the author. The play is dedicated to Hermann Hagedorn. Its seven characters are Van Zorn, George Lucas, Weldon Farnham, Otto Mink, Mrs Lovett, Villa Vannevar, and Jenny. Act one opens in Farnham's studio in Macdougal Alley, New York, with its long window, cushioned seat, screen, antique cabinet, and a bust of Shakespeare.

Farnham, a well-satisfied man of thirty, watches Otto study the portrait of Villa Vannevar on the easel. Otto, short, plump, pink, and talkative, concedes there is genius in it while doubting the likeness. Lucas and Petherick, he hears, think it rotten, though Lucas only smoked at it. Robinson, known for his poems of Tilbury Town, writes the talk dry and oblique, with character carried in what the men avoid saying.
78978-the-coach-horn:
The Coach-Horn tells the reader what to blow on a coach horn, and how to blow it. The writer signs as An Old Guard, a nod to the guard who rode at the back of the mail coach. The seventh edition came out in London.

The book comes from Köhler and Son, a London firm of instrument makers. The firm traces its craft back to 1780 and boasts royal favour. Its horns served the great age of horse drawn mail coaches. Calls for the road, the yard and the hunt fill such a guide. The book preserves a lost sound of old travel. Royal arms on the title page mark the maker's pride.
79574-ocean-born:
Oliver Optic's Ocean-Born, or The Cruise of the Clubs, closes the Yacht Club Series as its sixth and last volume. Lee and Shepard published it at Boston; the preface is dated Towerhouse, Boston, March 12, 1875. Optic explains that each series volume stands alone, and that these incidents are somewhat more romantic than the others, though not improbable. He muses that fiction holds only about half a dozen plot elements, permuted into every story.

Both the Yacht Club and the Dorcas Club appear, so the whole matter can conclude. Early chapters bring the Ocean-Born herself, a dismasted sloop, the fate of the Sea Foam, and a lost child. The hero sails a steam yacht but is a young man of high aims, the preface insists, worthy of imitation. Thirteen illustrations accompany the tale, one showing the crew clearing a broken spar.
a-little-swiss-sojourn: William Dean Howells records a little Swiss sojourn with illustrations. Tourists at Montreux, the White Cross Inn, Villeneuve, and the Castle of Chillon fill its pages. Scenes of haymaking, cattle at fountains, washing clothes in the lake, and a wine press follow. Howells writes a light travel sketch of Swiss life and scenery.
anahuac-or-mexico-and-the-mexicans-ancie: Edward Burnett Tylor writes Anahuac, or Mexico and the Mexicans, ancient and modern, with an introduction and itinerary for his travels. The book studies Mexican peoples old and new, their customs, ruins, and daily life, with an anthropologist's eye. Tylor's account remains a classic early work of scientific travel in Mexico.
beth-woodburn:
Maud Petitt published her first book with William Briggs of Toronto in 1897, dedicating it lovingly to her mother. Beth Woodburn is eighteen as the tale opens, the daughter of a doctor, dreaming of life and of the university. Chapters named Whither, Beth?, 'Varsity, Ended, and Death map the plot's arc: ambition, Toronto student days, love, and bereavement in a Canadian Methodist world.

Family memory fills the sampled scene. An old friend recalls Beth's father holding her in long dresses as a baby. When her sweet mother died, he came to comfort the child and filled her lap with flowers. Beth weeps silently until the doorbell calls Dr. Woodburn away. Petitt writes the earnest, churchly romance of a girl whose heavenly Canaan and earthly love must be reconciled before the farewell chapter.
books-and-habits-from-the-lectures-of-la:
John Erskine chose and edited Books and Habits in London in 1922, from the lectures of Lafcadio Hearn. Hearn had taught English letters to Japanese students, and Erskine, a Columbia professor, frames the talks with an introduction. The lectures speak straight to learners meeting a foreign culture in its books.

Hearn opens with the deep gap between Japanese and Western daily life, above all in the place of women. Later talks take up poems, songs, and small creatures like the butterfly as a sign of the soul. Coleridge and other English poets pass under his lens. Hearn reads with care for custom and feeling behind the words. Students of either country get a bridge built by a man who lived on both sides.
britannica-1911-abercarn: Abercarn is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names an urban district in Monmouthshire's southern division, north-west of Newport on the Great Western railway. Its people numbered 12,607 in 1901. The town lies in the middle reach of the Ebbw valley. Collieries, ironworks, and tinplate works fill the district, the entry states. It sits on the south-eastern flank of the great Glamorgan and Monmouth mining region, and its work and growth rest on coal and metal, as the brief gazetteer notice records.
britannica-1911-acorn:
Acorn is the fruit of the oak tree. Sailors use the word for a mast-head piece too. That piece keeps the vane in place. Its shape recalls the nut. The 1911 Britannica entry spends its space on word history. Earlier forms include akerne and acharn. The word derives from a Gothic term for fruit. It first meant fruit of the unenclosed land. The oak's crop was the most important forest produce.

Spelling drifted by folk etymology. People linked the word with corn. They also linked it with oak-horn. Chaucer writes of achornes of okes. The entry sends readers to the New English Dictionary. That work discusses the word's history at length. A humble nut carries a long linguistic trail.
britannica-1911-alpenhorn-alphorn:
Alpenhorn, or Alphorn, in the 1911 Britannica, is an instrument entry on the long wooden horn of Swiss hill folk. The tube is built from thin strips of birch, soaked till they bend, then wound into a cone. Bark covers the tube, and a cup shaped mouthpiece of hard wood tops it off. Length runs from four to eight feet. With no side holes, the horn gives the pure natural harmonic series.

The bore is slim for its length, so the high harmonics come with ease. The famed Ranz des Vaches is its stock tune. Beethoven wove that tune into his Pastoral Symphony, and Rossini used it in William Tell. Wagner, not content with the cor anglais for a herdsman's pipe in Tristan, had a wooden horn made with one valve for Bayreuth.
britannica-1911-baarn:
Baarn is a small town in the Dutch province of Utrecht, five miles by rail east of Hilversum. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as a summer resort set in fine woods, much liked by people from Amsterdam. The Baarnsche Bosch, a great wood, runs south from the town toward Soestdyk.

At Soestdyk stands a royal country seat first gained by the state in 1795. Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland, kept a collection of animals there until it was moved to Amsterdam in 1809. In 1816 the nation gave the estate to the prince of Orange for his service at Quatre Bras, and the palace has since grown larger and finer. Near the town stand the old castle sites of Drakenburg and Drakenstein and a notable dolmen at Vuursche.
britannica-1911-bannockburn:
Bannockburn is a town of Stirlingshire in Scotland, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the stream that gives it its name, the Bannock, a feeder of the Forth. The Gaelic words mean white, shining stream. Its people numbered 2,444 in 1901. At the start of the nineteenth century it was a village, and it now has brisk trades in woollens and leather.

The Bore Stone, in which Bruce set his flag before the great battle, is kept safe by an iron grate. A mile west is the Gillies' Hill, named for the camp followers whose show sealed the rout of the English. The famed battle was fought on the twenty-fourth of June 1314 for the relief of Stirling Castle. The English governor had sworn to yield the castle if no relief came by that day.
britannica-1911-barley-corn:
Barley-corn is a grain of barley, and from that grain an old measure was taken: its length, with three grains laid end to end, sometimes four, making up an inch. So the smallest of seeds gave English measure one of its oldest units.

The barley-corn has also been personified, made into a character, as the spirit of the malt liquor brewed from barley. The 1911 Britannica entry points to Burns's song John Barleycorn as the famous case, where the grain is ploughed, cut, and threshed like a suffering man, only to rise again as drink. The entry is very short, holding just the measure, the count of grains to the inch, and the song.
britannica-1911-bearn:
Bearn was a small frontier province in the south of France. The 1911 Britannica entry places it now in the department of Basses-Pyrenees. Soule and Lower Navarre bound it on the west side in old days. Chalosse, Tursan, and Astarac lay to its north in those times. Bigorre lay east, and the Pyrenees rose to the south of it.

Its name traces back to the town of Beneharnum, now Lescar. That town's folk formed a civitas in the Roman province there. Vascones conquered the land in the 500s and took it as their own. In 819 it became a viscounty under the dukes of Aquitaine. That feudal link broke in the 1000s as its lords grew free.
britannica-1911-blackburn:
Blackburn is a mill town and borough in Lancashire, England, 210 miles north-west by north from London. It stands in the valley of a small stream once called the Blackeburn, with hills rising to some 900 feet nearby. Its population grew from 120,064 in 1891 to 127,626 in 1901.

Cotton weaving is the town trade, and the entry says thousands worked in the mills, with iron founding and machine making close behind. Public buildings listed include the town hall of 1856, a free library, market house, and exchange, plus two large parks. Blackburn was incorporated in 1851, became a county borough in 1888, and sent two members to parliament.
britannica-1911-blackburn-colin-blackbur:
Colin Blackburn (1813–1896), later Baron Blackburn, was a British judge known as a leading voice on common law. Born in Selkirkshire, he studied at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, and took high maths honours in 1835. He was called to the bar in 1838 and rode the northern circuit.

His early practice was quiet and largely commercial, and he spent years editing law reports with T. F. Ellis. His move to the queen's bench in 1859 surprised many, yet he soon proved one of the soundest judges there. In 1876 he rose to the court of appeal and became a lord of appeal with a life peerage. His judgments, the entry says, were received with great respect.
britannica-1911-bokenam-osbern:
Osbern Bokenam (born 1393, died about 1447) was an English friar and poet who wrote lives of women saints in verse. By his own account he was born on 6 October 1393, perhaps at Bookham in Surrey. The closing note of his book calls him a Suffolk man, an Austin friar of Stoke Clare.

He travelled twice to Italy and made a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in 1445. His work is a set of thirteen legends of holy maids and women, mostly in seven- and eight-line stanzas, nine with prologues. A follower of Chaucer and Lydgate, he drew chiefly on the Legenda Aurea. Several legends were written for ladies who wanted their name-saints' stories. One copy alone survives, finished in 1447.
britannica-1911-buckthorn:
Buckthorn is a shrub known to botanists as Rhamnus cathartica. This 1911 Britannica article describes it and its kin. The plant grows much branched, to about 10 feet. Its bark is blackish and its twigs carry spines. Its leaves are oval with sharp serrated edges. The small green flowers come in sets of four parts. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. The fruit is black, round and juicy, with four stones.

Buckthorn is native across England, Europe and north Asia. In England it grows in woods on chalk soil. Its fruit acts as a strong purgative. Its bark yields a yellow dye. The article then covers allied species in turn. Berry-bearing alder gives a green dye from unripe fruit. Its soft wood serves for gunpowder making. Sea-buckthorn grows on sandy shores, with orange-yellow fruit. American kinds include the cascara sagrada of the Pacific coast.
britannica-1911-churn:
Churn, from the Old English cyrin and found in kindred forms across Teutonic tongues, is a vessel in which butter is made. Cream is shaken or beaten in it so that the fatty particles form butter and part from the buttermilk. Early churns were upright, shaped like the cans now used to carry milk, to which the name churn is also given. Those upright churns were worked by hand with a wooden plunger.

Later came a box-shaped churn with a splasher revolving inside, turned by a handle for the work. The modern churn in large dairies, worked by mechanical means, either revolves or swings itself as a whole. That motion returns to the oldest method of butter making known here. Cream was first shaken or swung in a skin bag or a gourd, long before dairy machines took over the task.
britannica-1911-cittern:
Cittern, also spelled cithern and in many kindred forms, is a medieval stringed instrument with a neck ending in a grotesque head, played by fingers or a plectrum. Its popularity stood at its height in England and Germany during the 16th and 17th centuries. The body is pear-shaped, like a lute's but with a flat back and soundboard joined by ribs. A fretted fingerboard runs along the neck, and the head curves under a carved woman's or animal's head.

Strings are of wire in pairs of unisons called courses, usually four in number in England. Tuning is peculiar, since the third course, called bass, sounds lower than the fourth, called tenor. Vincentio Galilei held England to be the birthplace of the cittern, the entry reports. Lesson books appeared in 17th century England, with Anthony Holborne's Cittharn Schoole of 1597 and Thomas Robinson's lessons of 1609 named as rare survivors.
britannica-1911-corn: Corn is a short word entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word is common to the Teutonic tongues. At first it meant a small hard bit or grain. It then came to name the hard seed of a plant. In farm use it names the seed of cereal plants. Local use fixes which grain the word points to. In England it means wheat most of all. In Scotland and Ireland it means oats in chief. In the United States it means maize alone.
britannica-1911-elmshorn:
Elmshorn is a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Schleswig-Holstein, on the river Krückau, 19 miles by rail north-west from Altona. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Elmshorn article within it. Its population in 1905 was 13,640. The entry is short and factual, naming the town's chief trades and its shipping.

Its industries include weaving, dyeing, brewing, and iron-founding. The town also makes leather goods, boots and shoes, and machines. A considerable shipping trade is carried on from the town. Beyond those points the entry gives no history or description of the place. Readers get a compact civic snapshot of a small industrial port town in the years just before the 1911 edition appeared, with its work and trade set out in a few lines.
britannica-1911-fehmarn:
Fehmarn is an island of Germany in the Baltic. It belongs to the Prussian province of Schleswig-Holstein. The Fehmarn-Sund, a strait less than a quarter of a mile wide, parts it from Holstein. The island is a gently rolling tract of about 120 square miles. It has no forest, but its pasture-land is excellent. Cattle are raised there in considerable numbers. Its population is given as 10,000.

The entry is very short, only a few lines long. It fixes the island's place in the Baltic and names the narrow strait. It gives the island's size and population. It also notes its one noted strength, rich grazing land and the cattle kept on it. Nothing more is offered in the hosted text. No towns, history or trade are described there.
britannica-1911-gaskell-elizabeth-clegho:
Elizabeth Cleghorn Gaskell (1810-1865) was an English novelist and biographer, born in Chelsea on 29 September 1810. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how her mother died a month after her birth, and she was raised at Knutsford in Cheshire by her aunt. That town, the entry notes, she later idealized in Cranford. In 1832 she married William Gaskell, a Unitarian minister in Manchester.

Her first novel, Mary Barton, a tale of Manchester life, appeared in 1848 and made her name. The entry follows her books in order, giving Cranford classic status and calling her Life of Charlotte Bronte, of 1857, one of the best biographies in the language. Later works include Sylvia's Lovers of 1863. She died on 12 November 1865, and her unfinished Wives and Daughters appeared in 1866.
britannica-1911-geldern:
Geldern, a town of Germany in Rhenish Prussia, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Niers, 28 miles north-west of Dusseldorf, where rail lines to Wesel and Cologne meet. Its people numbered 6,551 in 1905. It has one Protestant church, two Catholic churches, and a town hall with a fine council room.

Its trades are the making of buttons, shoes, cigars, and soap. The article dates the town from about 1100 and calls it early a strong fortified place. Until 1371 it was the seat of the counts and dukes of Gelderland. It passed to Spain, and Philip the Second made its walls stronger. Frederick the Great later razed those walls, the town having been Prussian since 1703. The entry closes with a list of German histories of the town.
britannica-1911-goulburn:
Goulburn is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a city in Argyle county, New South Wales, Australia. The city lies 134 miles south west of Sydney on the Great Southern railway. Its population in 1901 was 10,618. It stands at an altitude of 2,129 feet in a district the entry calls rich for farming.

The article presents Goulburn as the chief depot for the inland trade of the southern part of the state. It notes both Anglican and Roman Catholic cathedrals in the city. Local work included the making of boots and shoes, flour, and beer, along with tanning. The entry also gives two civic dates: a municipality formed in 1859 and city status gained in 1864.
britannica-1911-hohenzollern:
Hohenzollern is the name of a castle that stood on the hill of Zollern, south of Hechingen. It gave its name to the family to which the present German emperor belongs. A vague tradition links the house with the Colonna of Rome; a firmer one links it with the Burkhardingers, counts in Raetia in the early 10th century. The first firm mention of the name comes in Berthold's chronicle, on Burkhard and Wezil of Zollern, who died in 1061.

Wezil's line died out in 1194. The lasting branches descend from Burkhard's son Frederick, whose grandson Frederick III backed the Hohenstaufen. Frederick III married Sophia, heiress of Conrad, burgrave of Nuremberg, and succeeded him as burgrave about 1192. He died about 1200. In 1227 his sons divided the lands. Conrad took Nuremberg and founded the greater, Franconian branch. Frederick kept Zollern and the old lands, heading the Swabian branch.
britannica-1911-holborn:
Holborn is a central metropolitan borough of London, bounded by St Pancras, Finsbury, the City of London, Westminster and St Marylebone. Its population was 59,405 in 1901, over an area of 405 acres. Its main road runs east and west as Holborn Viaduct, High Holborn and New Oxford Street. The name comes not from a lost Old Bourne stream but from Hole-bourne, the stream in the hollow, meaning the Fleet itself.

Before the viaduct was built in 1869, the road fell and rose sharply across the Fleet valley. Holborn Bars, west of the viaduct, marked the City entrance where tolls were taken. Northward lies Bloomsbury, a fashionable quarter in the 18th century. Southward, St Giles in the Fields was long notorious for crime and poverty, and some of London's earliest plague cases of 1664–1665 occurred there. Its institutions include the Royal College of Surgeons and the Foundling Hospital, founded by Thomas Coram in 1739.
britannica-1911-hoorn:
Hoorn is a seaport in the province of North Holland, Holland. It stands on a bay of the Zuider Zee called the Hoornerhop. It is a junction station 23 miles by rail north by east of Amsterdam, on the line to Enkhuizen. A steam tram links it with that town as well. Its people numbered 10,647 in 1900. Hoorn stands out for its old-world air and for its fine gabled houses of the 16th and 17th centuries.

Many of those houses bear carved words and reliefs on their fronts. Some of them mark the battle on the Zuider Zee in 1573, when the Beggars beat the Spaniards under Count Bossu. Walks and gardens now ring the town in place of the old city walls. A few towers and gates, with old coats of arms on them, still stand.
britannica-1911-hopkins-edward-washburn:
Hopkins, Edward Washburn is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American scholar of Sanskrit. He was born in Northampton, Massachusetts, on the eighth of September 1857. He graduated at Columbia University in 1878 and studied at Leipzig. There he took his doctor's degree in 1881.

He taught at Columbia from 1881 to 1885, then at Bryn Mawr for ten years. In 1895 he became professor of Sanskrit and comparative language study at Yale. He served as secretary of the American Oriental Society and edited its journal. He gave many papers to that journal, above all on number and time in early Sanskrit texts. His books include works on caste in ancient India, on the lawbook of Manu, and on the religions of India. The Great Epic of India, from 1901, closes the list in the entry.
britannica-1911-kent-s-cavern:
Kent's Cavern, or Kent's Hole, is the largest of the English bone caves. It is famous for giving proof that man lived in Devon at the same time as animals now extinct or no longer native. The cave lies about a mile east of Torquay harbour. It winds deep into a hill of Devonian limestone.

Though long known in the district, it was not studied in a scientific way until 1825. In that year the Reverend J. McEnery found worked flints lying close with the bones of extinct mammals. He saw that they proved man's presence in Devonshire while those animals lived, but the idea was too new for his age to accept. His findings were later confirmed by Godwin Austen, and in the end by the British Association's committee, whose diggings ran under Wm. Pengelly from 1865 to 1880.
britannica-1911-kinghorn:
Kinghorn is a royal and police burgh of Fifeshire, Scotland, with 1,550 people in 1901. It stands on the Firth of Forth, on the North British railway. Its public buildings include a library and a town hall. The town has some name as a summer resort. Its chief trades are ship-building, bleaching, and the making of flax and glue. In the time of Daniel Defoe, thread-making was in vogue there. That work kept the women busy while the men were at sea.

Alexander III made Kinghorn a burgh, but his tie with the town proved fatal to him. As he rode from Inverkeithing on 12 March 1286, his horse threw him. He fell over the cliffs west of the town and was killed. A stone was set up in 1887 to mark the spot where the fall is thought to have been.
britannica-1911-lambourn:
Lambourn is a market town in the Newbury division of Berkshire, 65 m. W. of London and the terminus of the Lambourn Valley light railway from Newbury. Its population in 1901 was 2071. It lies high up the narrow valley of the Lambourn, a tributary of the Kennet famous for its trout-fishing, among the Berkshire Downs. The church of St Michael is cruciform and mainly late Norman, with many later additions and much modern restoration. Inmates of an almshouse founded by John Estbury about 1500 still hold service daily at his tomb in the church, as he desired, and a Perpendicular market-cross stands outside.

The town has agricultural trade, but its chief importance comes from the large training stables in the neighbourhood. North of the town lies the group of tumuli called the Seven Barrows, shown by excavation to be a British burial-place.
britannica-1911-lantern:
Lantern, in the 1911 Britannica, is a metal case with clear sides. The case holds a light. It guards the flame from rain and wind. Two kinds are named: hanging and hand. Both are old. Bronze finds at Pompeii and Herculaneum show the early form. Horn plates sat round the lamp inside.

Later pages trace the craft through fine metal work. Iron and brass served most often. Silver and gold came rarely. Glass grew cheap and pushed out horn, talc, and oiled paper. Paper lanterns from China and Japan fold flat when not in use. Feasts in both lands give them a place. The closing sections turn to projection. Magic lantern views, dissolving pictures, and ghost shows fill the last pages.
britannica-1911-leghorn:
Leghorn, known in Italian as Livorno, is the subject of a city entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a city of Tuscany, Italy, and chief town of its province. That province also covers the islands of Elba and Gorgona. The town is the seat of a bishopric and of Italy's only naval academy.

It was the third largest commercial port in the kingdom at that time. Set on the west coast south west of Pisa, it stands just above sea level. Population figures for town and commune in nineteen hundred one are both given. It is built along the shore on a healthy tract of fertile land.
britannica-1911-malvern:
Malvern is an inland spa town in Worcestershire, England. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties its fame to hills and springs. It climbs the east slopes of the Malvern Hills. Those hills rise sheer from the flat Severn plain below.

Pure air and famed waters draw health seekers to the town. Open air cure for chest patients runs on a large scale. The name covers a string of small towns along the hills. Great Malvern is the chief of that five mile line. Its priory church keeps a Norman nave and old glass. A hermit cell endowed by Edward the Confessor began it all. Malvern College, founded in 1862, ranks as a known public school. Springs at Malvern Wells and a pure Holy Well draw crowds.
britannica-1911-paderborn:
Paderborn is a town and bishop's see of Germany, in the Prussian province of Westphalia. It lies sixty-three miles north-east of Dortmund, on the rail line to Berlin. It had 26,468 people in 1905, of whom about eighty per cent were Roman Catholics. Its Latin name means the springs of the Pader. Near two hundred springs of that small stream rise in the town, under the cathedral itself.

The springs flow with such force that they drive mills within a few yards of their source. Much of the town was rebuilt after a great fire in 1875. The chief of its half dozen churches is the Roman Catholic cathedral. Its west part dates from the 1000s, its centre from the 1100s, and its east from the 1200s. It was restored in the early 1890s. Among its treasures is the silver coffin of St Liborius.
britannica-1911-tondern:
Tondern was a town in the German province of Schleswig Holstein, on the Widau river near the North Sea. It lay west of Flensburg and faced the isle of Sylt. The entry gives its count of folk in nineteen hundred as just over four thousand. In old days it was a sea port.

Trade in farm goods and beasts, plus a big horse fair, kept the town busy. Ships no longer came up the river, so goods moved through Hoyer by rail. The close notes two gold horns found near the town in past years. Both were stolen from a museum in eighteen two and never found.
britannica-1911-tyburn:
Tyburn is a buried London stream whose name means death to most ears. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the river and its gallows. The stream rose at Hampstead and ran south wholly underground now. Old lanes and a dip in Piccadilly still trace its course.

The Middlesex gallows took the Tyburn name from that ground. It stood near the modern Marble Arch at two great roads. Killings there reach back to the end of the twelfth century. Galleries around the gibbet sold seats at high prices. Pretenders, saints, and earls all died on that frame. Even Cromwell bones were hung there after the king return. The last hanging at Tyburn came in 1783. Newgate prison took over the grim work from that year.
britannica-1911-urn:
Urn, from the Latin urna, is a vessel or vase, most often with an egg shaped body and a foot, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short entry. The Roman urna was first a jar for carrying or drawing water. It was also the vessel into which voting tablets and lots were cast. From that use came the figure of the urn of fate, from which the lots of man's destiny are drawn. 

The ashes of the cremated dead were laid in cinerary urns, a custom kept up by the marble urns set on funeral monuments. The word also served as a measure of liquid, half an amphora, and in modern use it names the large heated vessels from which tea or coffee is drawn by a tap.
britannica-1911-whithorn:
Whithorn, a royal burgh in Wigtownshire, Scotland, is noted for its church history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The burgh held 1,118 people in 1901 and stands near the south tip of the Machers peninsula. One long street runs north and south through the town, with the town hall on it. A railway links it to Wigtown, some twelve miles north.

The town is famed for its link with St Ninian, the first Christian missionary to Scotland. He landed at the Isle of Whithorn, a small headland to the south east. There in 397 he built a church of stone and lime. Its white walls, set against dark huts of mud and wattle, won it the name Candida Casa, the White House. He dedicated the church to St Martin of Tours.
britannica-1911-yarn:
Yarn, the name for any textile fibre spun ready for weaving into cloth, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Only in a few odd cases, such as haircloth or wire, is fabric made without spun yarn first. Yarn varies widely in kind and worth. Its value turns on lustre, dyeing quality, fineness, strength, and smoothness. It also turns on stretch, even thickness, suppleness, and natural colour.

Yarn is classed as single, folded, and fancy. Twisted to the right it is called twist way, and to the left, weft way. Single yarn is fibre twisted together in spinning. Warp yarn should be strong, elastic, and smooth. Weft yarn has less twist and stays spongy. The raw material shapes the result. Cotton yarn, for instance, is usually dull and soft, with moderate strength. Combing and gassing brighten it, and mercerizing gives it a high lustre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-bene:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Benedictbeurn describes a Bavarian abbey in the Alps, about thirty miles south of Munich, formerly in the diocese of Augsburg. Tradition and tenth-century manuscripts ascribe its foundation in 740 to three noble brothers, Lanfrid, Wulfram and Eliland, acting under St. Boniface, then preaching in Bavaria.

The Huns destroyed the house in 955 or 973, and Wolfold restored it in 969 as a college of canons. Through Emperor Henry the Third, Abbot Ellinger and eleven monks from Tegernsee revived Benedictine rule there in 1031. The entry follows the abbey's later fortunes, its abbots and its standing among Bavarian monasteries, and settles its much-varied spelling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durandus-of-t:
Durandus of Troarn was a French Benedictine and church writer born about 1012 near Evreux. He died at Troarn near Caen in 1089. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he was given from childhood to the communities of Mont-Sainte-Catherine and Saint-Vandrille. William, Duke of Normandy, made him abbot of the new Saint-Martin of Troarn, esteeming him alongside Lanfranc, Anselm, and Gerbert.

Ordericus Vitalis calls him a most skilled teacher of church song and doctrine, though of his music nothing survives but the praise. His Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord answers Berengarius, and its ninth part holds precious history of the heretic. The entry adds his epitaphs for Abbot Ainard and Countess Mabile, preserved by Migne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-born:
The first-born son held pride of place in ancient Israel, with a double share and his father's blessing. Before the Law, the birthright also carried a right to the priesthood of the household. First-born sons and firstling animals were held to be God's in a special way. Among nomad tribes this belief likely gave rise to sacrificing the first-cast animals.

Under the Law, every first-born son was redeemed one month after birth for five sicles. The payment went to the clergy and recalled the slaying of Egypt's first-born at the Exodus. The firstling of clean animals was sacrificed at a year old; unclean animals were redeemed with money. Polygamy forced precise rules on which child counted as first-born and which child was redeemed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-freiherr-max-:
Max von Gagern, a Nassau statesman born in 1810, spent the revolutionary year of 1848 trying to unite Germany under Prussia without Austria. Son of a Nassau minister, he studied law at Heidelberg, Utrecht, and Göttingen. He served the Dutch king, fought against Belgium in 1830, and later taught history at Bonn. He entered the Catholic Church in August 1843.

His conversion grew from reading Thomas à Kempis, Möhler, and the New Testament, and it cost him nothing with his duke. In 1848 he mediated between governments and people, chaired a committee of seventeen revising the constitution, and served as under-secretary for foreign affairs. When Prussia refused the imperial crown, he withdrew from the Frankfurt parliament with his party.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gertrude-of-h:
Gertrude of Hackeborn, Cistercian Abbess of Helfta, made her convent Germany's home of asceticism and mysticism. Born near Halberstadt in 1232 to the noble Hackeborns and sister to Saint Mechtild, she entered Rodersdorf young and was elected abbess in 1251 aged nineteen. In 1253 she founded Hedersleben with her brothers Albert and Louis.

Wanting water, Gertrude obtained her brothers' castle of Helfta and moved her community there in 1258. Under her rule Helfta became Germany's most famous abode of asceticism and mysticism, its nuns trained in liberal arts and above all in Scripture. A model abbess for piety and prudent direction, she bore apoplexy in her last eighteen months with heroic patience until her death near the end of 1292. She must not be confused with Saint Gertrude the Great, an ordinary nun of the same house born over twenty years later. For this abbess wrote nothing, claimed no revelations, and was never canonized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-goulburn:
Goulburn is one of the six suffragan sees of the ecclesiastical province of Sydney in New South Wales, Australia. Its episcopal city, population 10,612 in 1901, straddles the Sydney-Melbourne railroad at 2071 feet above the sea. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese watered by the Murrumbidgee, Murray, and Lachlan.

Formed as a separate diocese in 1864 from Sydney, it first went to Bonaventure Geoghegan, who died in Ireland that year without taking possession. His successor William Lanigan, consecrated at Goulburn in 1867, was the first Australian bishop consecrated in his own cathedral and an ardent promoter of Catholic education. By November 1908 the diocese counted fifty-nine priests, twenty-four parochial districts, and hundreds of sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-anton-z:
Jacob Anton Zallinger zum Thurn was a philosopher and canonist from Bozen. He was born there on 26 July 1735. He died there on 11 January 1813. He studied at Innsbruck and Munich. He joined the Jesuits on 9 October 1753. He was ordained priest on 1 June 1765. He then taught philosophy at Munich, Dillingen, and Innsbruck.

After the Jesuits were suppressed in 1773, Prince-bishop Clemens Wenceslaus hired him. He taught canon law at Augsburg for thirty years, from 1777 to 1807. He spent four months as theologian at the Ratisbon nunciature. He also spent sixteen months in Rome as papal councillor on German affairs. As a canonist he defended papal rights against Febronian trends. As a philosopher he favored Newton's empiricism over Scholastic method.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-pfef:
Johannes Pfefferkorn was a converted Jew whose campaign against Jewish books set off the great Reuchlin controversy. Born probably at Nuremberg in 1469, he was baptized at Cologne in 1505 with his wife and children, then pressed for the conversion of the Jews. His Judenspiegel of 1507 urged Jews to give up usury, work for a living, attend Christian sermons, and abandon the Talmud, while condemning persecution as a bar to conversion.

Convinced that Jewish books were the root of Jewish obstinacy, he won an imperial order in 1509 to seize them and began confiscations at Frankfurt, Worms, Mainz, and other towns. A second mandate put the affair under the Archbishop of Mainz, who sought opinions from universities and from Johann Reuchlin. Reuchlin defended all but openly offensive books, and the quarrel with Pfefferkorn and the Cologne Dominicans became a landmark dispute over learning, tolerance, and the treatment of Jews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-annega:
Joseph Annegarn was a German Catholic theologian and popular writer who lived from 1794 to 1843. Born at Ostbevern in Westphalia, he became professor of church history at the Lyceum Hosianum in Braunsberg, East Prussia, where he died. His service to German Catholic letters came chiefly through a history written for young readers and the general public.

His Universal History, published in eight volumes between 1827 and 1829, told world history from a frankly Catholic view in a bright, pleasing style. Character sketches of great figures and chronological tables were its best features, and later editors kept it current, so it stayed a standard book in German Catholic homes. He also wrote a handbook of patrology, the study of the Church Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-gasser:
Joseph Gasser von Valhorn was an Austrian sculptor who lived from 1816 to 1900. Born at Prägraten in Tyrol, he learned woodcarving from his father, studied at the Vienna Academy, and spent years in Rome on a government stipend. Settled in Vienna from 1852, he carved five heroic figures for Speyer Cathedral's portal and reliefs for its Kaiserhalle.

His other works include statues for the Arsenal museum, the Seven Liberal Arts for the Opera House staircase, and twenty-four figures for St. Stephen's Cathedral. His finest group serves Vienna's Votive Church: the Coronation of Mary, the Trinity, and Christ the Redeemer. He taught at the Academy from 1865 to 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lantern:
In modern architecture a lantern is a small structure crowning a dome to let in light, aid ventilation, and ornament the building. The name also covers any such projection, even one with no openings that serves decoration alone.

Examples span Europe and beyond: the Karlskirche in Vienna, St. Peter's in Rome, St. Paul's in London, St. Isaac's in St. Petersburg, Santa Maria della Salute in Venice, Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence, the Frauenkirche in Dresden, Val de Grace in Paris, St. Stephen's Walbrook in London, La Superga in Turin, and Palermo cathedral, with others at Montepulciano, Loyola, Genoa, and Guadalupe in Mexico.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lectern:
A lectern, from Latin legere, to read, is a bookstand, a solid permanent structure holding the large heavy Sacred Books for ministers at liturgical functions. Early churches used one only, later two: one at the choir's north wall, another opposite.

From the first, the priest preached and the bishop spoke, unless from his cathedra. Synod decrees were proclaimed there, censures and excommunications pronounced, diptychs read, and the deacon chanted the Gospel and his own liturgical parts. The second, longer but lower, split into two levels. The higher, facing the altar, served the subdeacon's Epistle. The lower, facing the nave, served other lessons. Some were marble, others wood adorned with silver, gold, enamel, gems, bronze, and ivory, and eagle-shaped lecterns spread widely in thirteenth- and fourteenth-century England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liesborn:
Liesborn was a noted former Benedictine Abbey in Westphalia, Germany, begun in 815 and suppressed in 1803. More likely two laymen, Bozo and Bardo, built it in 815. As time passed the nuns grew worldly, so in 1131 Bishop Egbert of Munster expelled them and put Benedictine monks in their place.

From the thirteenth century ascetic life declined as its wealth grew. The Bursfeld Union worked here in 1465 for discipline's restoration. To it Liesborn owed its flourishing state under abbots Heinrich of Cleves (1464-1490) and Johann Smalebecker, abbot 1490-1522, who restored the buildings and improved its economics. Abbot Heinrich's fine altar-paintings became famous, but under French rule in 1807 they sold for a mere song. Bernard Witte, a monk from 1490 to about 1534, wrote a history of Westphalia and an abbey chronicle. Under Johann Rodde (1582-1601) decay grew again, and things were worse during the seventeenth century's wars, until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malvern:
Malvern was a district in Worcestershire under a lofty range between the Severn and the Wye, the Malvern Hills. On the range's eastern side stood two Benedictine houses, the priories of Great and Little Malvern. This entry follows both houses through their tangled fortunes.

Great Malvern grew up soon after St Werstan's death; the Deerhurst monk was slain by Danes in the woods and honoured as a saint. A hermitage predated the Conquest, and Aldwyn, a Worcester monk, with a companion named Guy, first settled the site. At St Wulstan's counsel Aldwyn dropped a planned Jerusalem pilgrimage and began a monastery, gathering thirty monks. Later a bishop's harsh claims sparked long litigation, with monks at last under royal protection, until a truce at Acton Burnell freed them from his jurisdiction. Little Malvern, founded from Worcester about 1171, keeps only its choir and tower today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osbern:
Osbern of Canterbury was a monk, prior of Christ Church, and writer of saints' lives who died probably between 1088 and 1093. Brought up by Godric, dean from 1058 to 1080, he was ordained by Archbishop Lanfranc and grew skilled in music. Two music treatises are linked to his name, though his fame rests on hagiography, the writing of saints' lives.

William of Malmesbury praised the elegance of his style. Osbern turned Anglo-Saxon lives into Latin and wrote fresh ones of his own. His works include lives of Alphege and Dunstan, with a book of Dunstan's miracles, and a life of Archbishop Odo that has perished. A life of Dunstan printed under his name in Mabillon probably belongs to Eadmer instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paderborn:
Paderborn is a suffragan diocese of Cologne, taking in Minden and Arnsberg in Westphalia, Prussian Saxony, five Rhine districts, Lippe, Waldeck, Gotha, both Schwarzburgs, and the Vicariate Apostolic of Anhalt. It holds 53 deaneries, 547 parishes, 1,403 secular priests, 93 regular priests, 1,508,000 Catholics, and 5,250,000 non-Catholics. The diocese is large and mixed, with Catholics a minority among its people.

The cathedral chapter elects the bishop, and diocesan schools include a priests' seminary, an institute of philosophy and theology, the Leoninum college, and boys' seminaries at Paderborn and Heiligenstadt. Catholic charities run 120 child-protection homes, 50 orphan asylums, and many trade schools. Later pages trace the bishops from early foundations through the Thirty Years War to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-kentige:
Kentigern, also called Mungo, meaning dear one, was bishop and founder of the see of Glasgow. He was born about 518 and died at Glasgow on 13 January 603. His mother Thenaw was daughter of the British prince Lothus, and his father's name is unknown.

Brought up by Serf at Culross in Fife, according to Jocelyn's life, he began mission work at twenty-five at Cathures on the Clyde, the site of modern Glasgow. King Roderick of Strathclyde welcomed him and had him consecrated bishop about 540. He lived austerely in a cell where the Clyde meets the Molendinar, and a community called Clasgu, the dear family, grew around him into the town of Glasgow. Driven out about 553, he founded a monastery at Llanelwy, now Saint Asaph's, and returned after the battle of Arthuret in 573.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schaftlarn:
Schäftlarn, once Premonstratensian and now Benedictine, is an abbey on the Isar not far from Munich in Upper Bavaria. Priest Waltrich founded it in 762 for St Dionysius and served as first abbot, later becoming bishop of Passau from 774 to 804. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a house destroyed, refounded, secularised, and reborn.

Hungarians wrecked the monastery in 955 during their raids into Germany. In the eleventh century secular canons held it, until Bishop Otto of Freising refounded it in 1140 as a Premonstratensian house under a provost. Fire destroyed it in 1527, the provostry became an abbey in 1598, and secularisation ended it in 1803. After years as a girls' school, King Louis I bought it in 1865 and restored Benedictine life in 1866.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schonborn:
Schönborn names a German noble family rich in church prelates, above all Johann Philipp von Schönborn, who ruled Mainz as archbishop and held the bishoprics of Würzburg and Worms. Born at Eschbach in the Westerwald on 6 August 1605, he died at Würzburg on 12 February 1673. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a prince-bishop of the Thirty Years' War aftermath.

At sixteen he became an expectant cleric at Würzburg cathedral, then at Mainz in 1625. He became canon at Würzburg in 1629 and Worms in 1630, and provost of Kronberg and St Burkard in 1635. Bishop of Würzburg in 1642, deacon that year and priest in 1645, he became archbishop of Mainz in 1647 and bishop of Worms in 1663. His foreign policy sought peace, often without success or applause, but his home rule was excellent, earning him the titles Wise, German Solomon, and Cato of Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solomon-islan:
The Northern Solomon Islands prefecture covered Ysabel, Choiseul, Bougainville, and the smaller islets under German protection in the western Pacific. This entry records its early mission years. Placed under the vicar apostolic of Samoa in 1897, it became a prefecture of its own in 1898. Mgr Joseph Forestier led it from Kieta on Bougainville.

By 1911 the mission counted three churches and three stations. It had Marist fathers and lay brothers, sisters of the Third Order of Mary, and Samoan catechists. Five schools taught 140 pupils, and two orphanages served a few hundred Catholics. Fever, the entry notes frankly, had already carried off most of the fathers who arrived in 1898. That loss is a grim reminder of the human cost of the work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sze-ch-wan-ea:
Eastern Sze-ch'wan became a Vicariate Apostolic in 1856, after separation from the northwest, and was first called South-eastern Sze-ch'wan. Nine European and ten native priests served it under its first vicar, Desflèches, bishop of Sinita, who led it from 1844 to 1887. Early years brought heavy persecution, until the Franco-Chinese War of 1860 won full freedom to preach.

In 1860 the mission split into Eastern and Southern vicariates, and Chinese officials granted land at Ch'ung-k'ing as compensation for losses. Fresh violence followed: priests were jailed and murdered, settlements were pillaged in 1876, and mission buildings at Ch'ung-k'ing were wrecked in 1886. By 1910 the Paris Foreign Missions vicariate counted 40,587 Catholics, 341 schools, and 175 churches under Bishop Chouvellon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sze-ch-wan-no:
North-western Sze-ch'wan covers Ch'wan-si and Ch'-wan-pe, with Kiong-chu, Ya-y-hien, Mu-pin, and part of Tsechu prefecture, among 25,000,000 people, of whom 23,000,000 are Chinese and 1,500,000 Man-tse. Rome entrusted the whole Sze-ch'wan mission to Bishop Pallu in 1658, but neither he nor his successor Lyonne could enter the province. Only in 1707 did Paris missionaries and Vincentians reach it.

La Balluère, elected vicar in 1713, died before consecration, Mullener was consecrated in 1717, and four later electees never reached consecration at all. Real organized life dates only from Bishop Pottier, consecrated in 1769, when the mission counted about 4,000 Christians. Persecution, banishment, and a synod that completed its organization followed, and by 1910 it counted 45,000 Catholics with 340 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sze-ch-wan-so:
Southern Sze-ch'wan became a Vicariate Apostolic on 24 January 1860, separated from the east by decree of Pius IX. Its first vicar, Pichon, bishop of Heliopolis, began with 12,000 Catholics, himself the only European missionary, plus three native priests and four chapels. He founded a seminary at Ho-ti-keou in 1862 and died in France in 1871, succeeded by Lepley.

Violence scarred the mission: Protestant buildings at Chen-tu fell in May 1895, Catholic settlements followed the next day, and about half the mission's settlements were destroyed. A new persecution broke out in 1898, the Boxers spared it somewhat in 1900, and some thirty Christians were murdered between 1895 and 1904. By 1910, under Bishop Chatagnon at Sui-fu, it counted 36,618 Catholics and 280 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-master-of:
An unnamed Westphalian painter, known only by his masterpiece, is the subject of this art entry. In 1465 he painted a noted altar-piece for the Benedictine monastery of Liesborn, founded by Charlemagne. The monastery's historian, silent on his name, judged that Greeks would have ranked him first among artists. Westphalia already rivalled Cologne in the fourteenth century.

Against Stephen Lochner of Cologne, the Liesborn master holds his own, sharing with him and the Van Eycks a backward-looking grace rather than a forward thrust. Suppression in 1807 scattered the altar-piece, sold and split into fragments now in London's National Gallery, Münster Museum, and private hands. A copy at Luenen hints at its lost glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-win:
Walter of Winterburn was an English Dominican cardinal, orator, poet, philosopher, and theologian of the thirteenth century, dying at Genoa on 26 August 1305. Entering the Dominicans young, he became renowned for learning, prudence.

In 1305, after helping elect Clement V, he set out from Perugia with other cardinals to join the pope in France. Fell mortally ill at Genoa, attended by Nicholas de Prato, dean of the Sacred College. First buried in his order's Genoa church, his remains were later transferred to London as he had ordered, to the convent where he had served. His friend Nicholas Trivet testifies to his many superior qualities, rare modesty, kindly disposition, and mature learning, and to prayer hours never shortened despite cloister and court duties. His chief works include a commentary on the Sentences and theological questions much used in his day.
doe-osti-2585504-a-short-survey-of-curre:
David Kittell leads a thirteen-author Sandia National Laboratories team in report SAND2025-09228, printed July 25, 2025. Antonio Garcia, Michael Hobbs, William Erikson, and nine colleagues join him in surveying reactive burn models as of mid-2025. Burn models describe how an explosive's reaction front grows and releases energy inside hydrocode simulations of shocks and detonations.

The survey began as a concise memo and grew into a short report for readers who already run burn models. It lays out the current state of the art and names the gaps the authors see in present capability. The team aimed for brevity, clarity, and utility, so the document works as a quick reference. A note in the abstract flags why the date matters: advances in artificial intelligence could shift the field before the year ends.
doe-osti-2588783-flexible-fuel-electric-:
Libbey Glass LLC filed this Phase 1 performance report narrative for its Flexible Fuel Electric Hybrid Glass Furnace Demonstration, an Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations industrial award. Mike Lindsey, the company's chief financial officer, submitted it on April 30, 2025. The reporting period covers the first quarter of 2025, inside a first budget period running to June 30, 2025. No author is named in the catalog record; the narrative is the company's own.

Glass furnaces burn large amounts of fuel, and a hybrid that flexes between fuel and electric melting is the demonstration's point. Phase 1 is engineering, not construction: an engineering package taken to 30 percent design maturity, with integrated schedules, a Class III cost estimate, community benefits engagement, and environmental review paperwork. The Phase 1 budget is 1.44 million dollars at 50 percent cost share. Status signals rate scope and spend green and schedule yellow, tied to a Phase 2 application deadline and changes in the project team.
doe-osti-3000976-tracking-carbon-dioxide:
Nicole Lovenduski and Alison Gray close award DE-SC0022243 with a short accomplishments summary. It covers September 2021 to August 2025, on the Southern Ocean's appetite for carbon dioxide. That ocean soaks up a large share of human emissions, yet climate models disagree with observations on how much. The team chased the mismatch inside E3SM, the Energy Department's Earth system model.

They taught the model to carry simulated Biogeochemical-Argo floats. Those are drifting robots that profile real ocean chemistry. Two big simulations followed. One was a six-year global run with fine detail in the tropics. The other was a 63-year run refined around the Southern Ocean. Outputs were checked against float data and the CMIP6 model archive, to map where the modelled carbon flux goes wrong. Nine peer-reviewed papers came out of the work; three are highlighted. The hosted text is a compact final summary.
doe-osti-3004689-probabilistic-hazard-as:
D. Werth of Savannah River National Laboratory updates a site safety case in an October 2025 hazard assessment. It covers tornadoes, straight-line wind, and extreme precipitation at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina. Federal rules require the site's buildings to be designed against set return periods, so the odds of extreme weather must be computed, not guessed.

Using Georgia and South Carolina tornado records and a two-degree square around the site, the strike probability for any point at the site came out at 7.04 ten-thousandths per year, about one chance in 1,420. Design wind speeds were 132 miles per hour at a 50,000-year return period and 147 at 125,000 years. Rainfall tables run from 15-minute bursts to 24-hour totals. Results are compared with the site's 2013 assessment.
doe-osti-3009034-the-hydropower-game-an-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-25/61, dated January 2026, documents the Hydropower Game, an interactive learning tool built for the Water Power Technologies Office. Its authors are Quentin Ploussard, Elise DeGeorge, Lukas Livengood, and six co-authors. It aims at the future hydropower workforce.

Players enter the fictional Blue Rapids plant, where a senior engineer mentor tours them through the turbine room in an opening level with no challenges, just orientation. Level 1 teaches run-of-river generation through a simple rule: power output scales with the water release rate through the turbine. Later levels build decisions on that base, turning plant operation into playable problems.
doe-osti-3487001-cloud-based-demonstrati:
Pacific Northwest report dated June 2026 demonstrates ESAMS, an Eastern Interconnection monitoring system, running in the cloud. James D. Follum of the lab leads authors from ISO New England, PJM, Electric Power Group, and Amazon Web Services. The system watches grid conditions across the East.

Cloud security tools can be applied in a set, repeatable way, the report argues. Identity controls, network splits, and encryption at rest and in transit head the list. Shared standards help many firms deploy one system together. Grid operators gain a path to shared awareness tools without building private data centers.
english-literature-modern:
G. H. Mair surveys the modern centuries in English Literature: Modern, a Home University Library volume first printed in 1911 and revised in 1914. Ten chapters run from the Renaissance through Elizabethan poetry and the drama to the present age. The novel gets a chapter of its own, and a bibliography and chronological table close the book.

Mair opens with the widening of knowledge that marks great ages, like a revelation in one man's life. He gives Swift his due, noting what Swift learned from Temple's easy urbanity and polish. Mair, sometime scholar of Christ Church, writes a small book with a clear map. It suits the home student who needs the whole modern field in one short volume.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Cub:
United States trade sanctions on Cuba reached their sixtieth year, and the Archive marked the date by posting its own documents on the embargo's start. One early statement of intent is quoted in full. The goal was to bring about hunger, desperation, and the overthrow of the Castro government.

That plain wording is why the posting matters. Sanctions are often defended in mild language about pressure and change. The founding documents say something harsher, aimed at daily life on the island. Readers can judge six decades of policy against the purpose its authors wrote down at the beginning.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Early Atomic Energy Commission studies warned that gas centrifuges could spread nuclear weapons with ease. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 385, published in June 2012. The studies said it would not be too difficult to build a secret plant producing highly enriched uranium.

Unless the United States and its allies imposed classification and export controls, officials feared, unfriendly countries such as China could acquire centrifuges. History proved the warning right: centrifuge technology later powered several secret programs. Reading the early studies shows the risk was understood in detail decades before it dominated headlines, and that controls were the chosen answer from the start.
john-barleycorn:
John Barleycorn is Jack London's book about his own life with alcohol, published in 1913. John Barleycorn is the old name for drink itself, treated here as a person. The book opens on an election day in California's Valley of the Moon. London rides down from his ranch to vote, taking several drinks before and after his ballot.

At supper, his wife Charmian asks why he voted for women's suffrage. He answers at length: women, he says, will vote for prohibition and drive nails into John Barleycorn's coffin. Yet he calls drink both the king of liars and the frankest truth-teller. That split feeling, friend and foe at once, drives this honest memoir of a drinking life.
life-of-johnson-volume-5-tour-to-the-heb:
Volume Five holds Boswell's Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides. Johnson accompanied him through Scotland in 1773. The volume adds Johnson's diary of a journey into North Wales in 1774. Hill's six-volume edition frames both travel records together.

Boswell's journal prints poems by Johnson about the tour. Conversations, literary anecdotes, and opinions of men and books follow. An authentic account covers the Jacobite grandson's distresses and escape in 1746. This third edition of the journal was revised and corrected. Poetical pieces by Johnson about the tour appear here first. The Jacobite escape account adds highland history to the travels.
prayers-written-at-vailima-and-a-lowden-:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Prayers Written at Vailima appear here with an introduction by his widow, in the Chatto and Windus edition of 1916, bound with his poem A Lowden Sabbath Morn. Stevenson wrote the prayers in Samoa for the evening service of his household at Vailima. His widow explains that every Samoan household closes the day with prayer and hymns, and that omitting the duty would shame the house chief. Her introduction compares the average Samoan to a larger child at his mother's knee, going to bed with a sense of heavenly protection.

The prayers themselves are short, plain, and tender, written to be spoken aloud by a family and its servants under a Samoan roof. A Lowden Sabbath Morn, a Scots poem of a quiet Sunday in the Lowlands, carries the homesick counterweight. Together they show the private Stevenson: the unbeliever's son who became, in exile, a patriarch of prayer.
publications-of-the-scottish-history-soc:
Donald Crawford edited the journals of Sir John Lauder, Lord Fountainhall, for the Scottish History Society in a volume dated May 1900. Lauder kept notes on public affairs and private matters between 1665 and 1676, a span of travel and early legal life.

The contents list a journal in France from 1665 to 1667, journeys in London, Oxford, and Scotland, a chronicle of the Court of Session, and remarks on public affairs. An appendix adds his accounts and a catalogue of his books. Readers get a young Scots lawyer's sharp record of courts, roads, and books.
star-born:
Andre Norton opens Star Born with a quote from Tas Kordov's Record of the First Years. What of our children, Kordov asks, the second and third waves born on this new world? They will hold no memories of Terra's green hills and blue seas. Will they be Terrans, or something else? Ace Books printed the novel at New York, and a note says deep searching found no proof that its copyright was renewed.

Chapter 1, Shooting Star, brings two travelers to a cove sighted from the sea. Dalgard steers an outrigger into the narrow break in the cliff wall, his paddle in time with Sssuri's in the bow. The two are neither of the same race nor of the same species, yet they work as one without words. Dalgard Nordis is a son of the Colony, whose Terran outlaw forebears fled foes across the galaxy to win a foothold on Astra.
the-adventures-of-captain-horn: Frank R. Stockton wrote The Adventures of Captain Horn. This copy is a 1910 printing. Its chapter list opens with An Introductory Disaster. The Rackbirds and Three Wild Beasts follow. The Captain Explores and A New Hemisphere come next. A Tradition and a Waistcoat stands midway. Mine, The Cliff-Maka Scheme, and Mrs. Cliff is Amazed close the parts shown.
the-fortunes-of-oliver-horn:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote The Fortunes of Oliver Horn as a novel of old Baltimore, giving the book to the memory of Richard Horn, a famed inventor little understood. Kennedy Square frames the tale.

Smith paints the square of the late fifties as a place of birds, trees, magnolias, and climbing roses. Boys and girls play by day while old gentlemen read in the shade. Watermelon men and oyster sellers work the pave outside the fence. In that soft, fading world the Horn family rises and falls, and young Oliver must make his way as art and trade change the town around him.
the-great-return: Arthur Machen wrote The Great Return. The Faith Press published it in London in 1915. Machen is named as author of The Bowmen. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a list of his other books, and a contents list. The contents name two pieces: The Rumour of the Marvellous and Odours of Paradise. No page of the tale itself is present. Its story cannot be told from what is here.
the-jewish-manual-practical-information-:
An anonymous lady edited this manual in London in 1846. It joins Jewish cookery with modern dishes. Hints on the toilette come with it. Her preface states the gap plainly. Many works on cookery existed already. None gave insight into the Hebrew kitchen. General cookbooks failed the Jewish housekeeper. Banned foods and mixes filled nearly every dish. Such books were useless to her.

The receipts came down by memory and manuscript. One generation of Jewish women passed them to the next. Plain English dishes join them here. French dishes from refined modern tables follow. Most were tested in the editor's own kitchen. Care went to accuracy and cheapness. Hard and costly methods were left out on purpose. Those belong to the confectioner, she says. Her aim was to guide the young Jewish housekeeper.
the-laughing-cavalier-the-story-of-the-a: Baroness Orczy published her tale of a Scarlet Pimpernel ancestor with Doran in New York in 1914. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The list names an apology and a prologue. Early chapters cover New Year Eve, a fracas by a postern gate, and watch night. The Dutch adventure itself, with its laughing cavalier and the brother and sister of later chapters, does not appear in this record.
the-lion-and-the-unicorn:
Richard Harding Davis gathers five war and adventure stories under his title piece. A florist named Prentiss keeps a shop in Jermyn Street, London, with a lion and a unicorn fixed over the front. Lodgings for single gentlemen fill the upper floors, as was usual on that street.

Captain Carrington moves in when the carved beasts arrive, and they watch his room by day and night. Maps and flag pins cover his table by day, while gold, silver, and soda bottles crowd it after dark. Other tales cover a fever ship, a vagrant, and a last ride together.
the-night-born:
Jack London's collection The Night-Born lists ten stories in its contents. The Madness of John Harned, When the World Was Young, The Benefit of the Doubt, Winged Blackmail, and Bunches of Knuckles follow the title story. War, Under the Deck Awnings, To Kill a Man, and The Mexican complete the set.

The title story opens in the old Alta-Inyo Club on a warm San Francisco night. Talk runs from the Graft Prosecution through the sordidness of man-hate until someone names O'Brien, the promising young pugilist who died in the prize-ring the night before. The air freshens at once: O'Brien neither drank, smoked, nor swore, and carried his prayer-book to the ringside. Old Trefethan, bald and dewlapped, takes up a Thoreau quotation and begins a tale from 1898.
the-outlaw-of-torn:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Outlaw of Torn, a tale of thirteenth-century England. The contents list nineteen chapters. In Chapter One the narrator explains that the story lay dormant for seven hundred years, first suppressed by a Plantagenet king, then forgotten. He found it among mildewed manuscripts in an ancient European monastery, through his wife's cousin, a Father Superior.

The manuscript records a remarkable revenge and the life of its innocent victim, Richard, the lost prince of England. Burroughs says he left out most of the history to follow the man at the center, a visored horseman. The events, he claims, shook England from north to south.
the-red-acorn: John McElroy is named as author on the electronic edition header. The header also gives the title. It gives an August 2001 release date. A later update followed in February 2018. Only that header is present on these pages. Its general notices appear with it. No part of the story itself appears here. Nothing about the plot can be told from these pages alone.
the-return:
Walter de la Mare opens in an old churchyard on a mild golden September afternoon, where Arthur Lawford wanders among stones in keen, mellow silence. Robins sing across the graves, and Lawford seems to himself the only living creature present.

A motto from Sir Thomas Browne warns against seeking wholesome flowers in a venomous plantation or risking contagion by nearness to corruption. Twenty-three untitled chapters are listed before the prose begins. Readers should not confuse this quiet, uncanny novel with the science fiction story of the same short title elsewhere in the set.
the-taming-of-red-butte-western: Francis Lynde wrote The Taming of Red Butte Western, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1910 and dedicated to Charles Augustine Stickle, his brother in deed if not by blood. Front matter and a contents list are all that this record holds. Sixteen chapters run from Collars-and-Cuffs and The Red Desert through outlaws, a killer, bridge-timbers, and blind signals, ending in a shadowgraph. One frontispiece line vows to spend a fortune finding a man and hanging him, which promises railroad-country revenge without delivering the story.
the-young-engineers-in-nevada-or-seeking:
Tom Reade meets a dough-faced boy of fourteen in The Young Engineers in Nevada, by H. Irving Hancock. The boy, Alf, asks whether Tom has the makings. He means tobacco makings, a bid toward manhood. Tom glances up in mild astonishment inside the tent. The contents promise gold fever, claim jumping, and wolves on snow. Jim Ferrers becomes the boys' partner in mining.

Nevada gold replaces railroads as the young engineers' pursuit. A goddess of fortune smiles wistfully in one chapter title. Dolph Gage fires a shot in another. Hancock mixes mining know-how with fights and rescues. Series readers follow Reade and Hazelton across the whole American West.
wild-western-scenes-a-narrative-of-adven: The title pages here give a full promise of contents for J. B. Jones's Wild Western Scenes, but the narrative itself does not start. Lippincott printed a revised stereotype edition in Philadelphia in 1875; Jones entered the book for copyright in 1856. The title page pledges tales of Daniel Boone, the great pioneer. It also promises bear, deer, and buffalo hunts, fights, wolf hunts, fishing, and encounters with serpents. Sixteen engravings from original designs illustrate the book. A preface begins at the foot of the pages shown.
woodside-or-look-listen-and-learn: Caroline Hadley wrote this children's nature book, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1902. Pages present here hold illustrated title pages and the start of a verse motto about Nature as an old nurse. The motto invites a child to wander and read the book of the natural world. Listed pictures promise a visit to a watchdog and an arrival at grandpapa's house. No story chapters appear in these pages.
